## 391. SEVENTH MEMORABLE RELATION. 
The nature of the desolation of truth and the theological famine <note>original: "macies." Literally a "leanness" or "wasting away," here referring to a lack of spiritual substance or knowledge.</note> in the Christian world today was made known to me from conversations with many of the laity and many of the clergy in the spiritual world; among these, there is such spiritual poverty that they hardly know anything except that there is a Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and that **Faith Alone** saves, and regarding the Lord Christ, only the historical facts about Him found in the Evangelists. As for the rest, which the Word of both Testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments of the Bible.</note> teaches about Him—such as that the Father and He are one; that He is in the Father and the Father in Him; that He has all power in heaven and on earth; that the Father’s will is that they believe in the Son, and that whoever believes in Him has eternal life—besides many more things, these are as unknown and hidden to them as things lying at the bottom of the ocean, or even in the center of the earth. And when these are brought forth from the Word and read, they stand as if hearing and yet not hearing; they enter no more deeply into the ears than the whispering of the wind or the sound of beaten leather. Angels, who are sometimes sent by the Lord to visit Christian societies in the world of spirits <note>In Swedenborg’s theology, the "World of Spirits" is an intermediate realm between Heaven and Hell where people go immediately after death.</note> beneath Heaven, lament greatly, saying that there is such obesity <note>original: "obesitas." Used here to mean spiritual dullness or a heart that has become insensitive and "fattened" against divine truth.</note> and resulting darkness in matters of salvation that it is almost like a speaking parrot. Even their learned men say that in spiritual and Divine matters they understand no more than statues. 

An Angel once told me that he spoke with two of the clergy, one who was in **Faith separate from Charity**, and another who was in <insert>|</insert> **Faith not separate**. He spoke with the one who was in faith separate from charity as follows: "Friend, who are you?" He replied, "I am a Reformed Christian." "What is your doctrine, and therefore your religion?" He replied that it is Faith. The angel said, "What is your faith?" He answered, "My faith is that God the Father sent the Son to take upon Himself the damnation of the human race, and that through this we are saved." He then asked, saying, "What more do you know about salvation?" He replied that salvation occurs through that faith alone. Furthermore he said, "What do you know about Redemption?" He replied that it was achieved through the **Passion of the cross**, and that His merit is imputed through that faith. Furthermore, "What do you know about Regeneration?" He replied that it happens through that faith. "Tell me what you know about Love and Charity?" He replied that they are that faith. "Tell me what you think about the precepts of the **Decalogue** <term>Decalogue</term><note>The Ten Commandments.</note> and the rest of the Word?" He replied that they are in that faith. Then the Angel said, "Therefore you will do nothing?" He replied, "What should I do? I cannot do good that is good from myself." The angel said, "Can you have faith from yourself?" He replied, "I do not inquire into this; I shall have faith." Finally the angel said, "Do you know anything else at all about salvation?" He replied, "What else, when salvation is through that faith alone?" But then the Angel said, "You answer like one who plays a flute with only one tone; I hear nothing but faith. If you know that and nothing else, you know nothing. Go and see your companions." And he went away and came upon them in a desert where there was no grass; he asked why it was so, and it was said, "Because there is nothing of the Church in them."

The Angel spoke with the one who was in **Faith conjoined to Charity** as follows: "Friend, who are you?" He replied, "I am a Reformed Christian." "What is your doctrine, and therefore your religion?" He replied, "Faith and Charity." The angel said, "These are two things." He replied, "They cannot be separated." The angel said, "What is Faith?" He replied, "To believe what the Word teaches." The angel said, "What is Charity?" He replied, "To do what the Word teaches." The angel said, "Have you only believed those things, or have you also done them?" He replied, "I have also done them." The Angel of Heaven then looked at him and said, "My friend, come with me and dwell with us."

## GOOD WORKS.

392. Faith has been dealt with; now Charity follows, because Faith and Charity are joined together just as Truth and Good are, and these two are like Light and Heat in the time of spring. This is said because Spiritual Light, which is the Light proceeding from the Sun of the spiritual world, is Truth in its essence; for this reason, Truth in that world, wherever it appears, shines with a brilliance according to its purity. And Spiritual Heat, which also proceeds from that Sun, is Good in its essence. These things are stated because the relationship between Charity and Faith is the same as that between Good and Truth; for Charity is the <term>complexus</term> <note>Latin for "the total embrace" or "the sum total." Swedenborg uses this to mean the entire collection of all possible good actions.</note> of all the Good that a person does for the Neighbor, and Faith is the sum total of all the Truth that a person thinks concerning God and Divine things. Since, therefore, the Truth of faith is Spiritual Light, and the Good of charity is spiritual Heat, it follows that the relationship between these two is the same as that between the two things of the same name in the Natural World; namely, that from their conjunction all things flourish upon the Earth, and in the same way, from their conjunction all things flourish in the human Mind. But there is a distinction: on the Earth, the blossoming is produced by natural Heat and Light, but in the human Mind, the blossoming is produced by Spiritual Heat and Light. Because this blossoming is spiritual, it constitutes Wisdom and Intelligence. There is also a correspondence between them; for this reason, the human Mind—in which Charity is joined to Faith, and Faith to Charity—is likened in the Word <note>The Bible.</note> to a Garden, and is also understood by the "Garden of Eden." That this is so has been fully shown in the *Heavenly Secrets* <note>original: "ARCANIS CÆLESTIBUS." This refers to Swedenborg's eight-volume theological work published in London between 1749 and 1756.</note> published in London. Furthermore, it should be known that unless Charity is dealt with after Faith has been dealt with, it is impossible to comprehend what Faith is; because, as was said and shown in the preceding Chapter, Faith without Charity is not Faith, nor is Charity without Faith truly Charity, and neither has life except from the Lord (see numbers 355 to 361). Also, the Lord, Charity, and Faith make one, just as Life, Will, and Understanding do; and if they are divided, each one perishes like a union crumbled into dust (see numbers 362 to 367). And moreover, Charity and Faith are present together in Good works (see number 373 and following).

393. It is a constant truth that Faith and Charity cannot be separated if a person is to have spiritual life and, as a result, salvation. That this is so is obvious to the Understanding of any person, even one not polished by talents and "minas" <note>A "mina" was an ancient unit of weight and currency; here it is a metaphor for scholarly "wealth" or intellectual equipment.</note> of learning. Who does not see from a certain inner perception, and agree with their understanding when they hear it...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Charity (living well) and Faith (believing rightly). It moves from the general definition of Charity to a psychological and spiritual analysis of the three fundamental loves that drive human behavior.</meta>

<page-num>261</page-num>

<header>OF THE NEW HEAVEN AND THE NEW CHURCH.</header>

<sig>Kk 3</sig>

Imagine someone saying, *That whoever lives well and believes rightly is saved*: who would not accept this? But who does not reject from their understanding—as if a grain of dust had fallen into the eye—the claim that *Whoever believes rightly, but does not live well, is also saved*? This is because an inner perception immediately triggers the thought: how can anyone truly believe rightly while not living well? What is such a faith then, except the mere outline of a painted faith, rather than a living image of it? 

Similarly, if someone were to hear, *That whoever lives well, even if they do not believe, is saved*, would not the Understanding, as it turns this over and reflects upon it, see and perceive that this does not hold together either? To live well is from God; for every good thing that is good in itself is from God. What then is "living well" without "believing," except like clay in the hand of a potter? It cannot be formed into a vessel for use in the spiritual Kingdom, but only for use in the natural Kingdom. Furthermore, who does not see the contradiction in those two statements—namely, *That one is saved who believes but does not live well*, and *That one is saved who lives well but does not believe*? Now, because "living well" (which belongs to Charity) is both known and unknown today—it is known what it means to live well naturally, but not what it means to live well spiritually—this subject of Charity will now be dealt with, organized distinctly into a series of Articles.

## That there are three universal Loves: the Love of Heaven, the Love of the World, and the Love of Self.

394. We begin with these three Loves because they are the universal and fundamental roots of all things, and because Charity has something in common with each of them. By <term>LOVE OF HEAVEN</term> <note>original: "Amor Caeli"</note> we mean love for the Lord and also Love toward the neighbor; and because both of these look toward use as their goal, it can be called the Love of Uses. <term>LOVE OF THE WORLD</term> <note>original: "Amor Mundi"</note> is not only the love of riches and possessions, but also the love of everything the world provides to delight the bodily senses: such as beauty for the eyes, harmony for the ears, fragrance for the nose, delicacies for the tongue, softness for the skin, as well as elegant clothing, comfortable homes, and social company—in short, all the delights arising from these and many other objects. <term>LOVE OF SELF</term> <note>original: "Amor Sui"</note> is not only the love of honor, glory, fame, and high status, but also the love of seeking and striving for offices, and thus of ruling over others. Charity has something in common with each of these three loves because Charity, viewed in itself, is the love of <term>uses</term> <note>In Swedenborg’s terminology, "uses" are the good works or services a person performs for the benefit of others, the community, or the Lord’s kingdom.</note>; for charity wishes to do good for the neighbor, and "good" is the same as "use." Each of these loves looks to uses as its goals: the Love of Heaven looks to spiritual uses, the Love of the World to natural uses (which may be called civil uses), and the Love of Self to corporeal uses (which may also be called domestic uses, for oneself and one's own).

395. These three Loves have been in every human being from creation and thus from birth. When they are rightly subordinated, they perfect the person, but when they are not, they pervert the person. This will be demonstrated in the following Article; here it is only necessary to mention that these three loves are rightly subordinated when the Love of Heaven forms the **head**, the Love of the World the **chest and belly**, and the Love of Self the **feet and the soles of the feet**. The human mind is divided into three regions, as has been said several times before: from the highest region, a person looks toward God; from the second or middle region, toward the World; and from the third or lowest region, toward themselves. Because the Mind is structured this way, it can be raised upward toward God and Heaven, it can be spread out sideways in every direction into the World and its nature, and it can be lowered downward toward the earth and toward hell. In this, the sight of the body emulates the sight of the mind; for it too can look up, look around, and look down. The human mind is like a house with three stories connected by stairs: in the highest story dwell the Angels from Heaven; in the middle, humans from the World; and in the lowest, spirits...

when these loves are rightly subordinated <note>ordered in a hierarchy of importance</note>, a person can ascend and descend at will. When they ascend to the highest dwelling, they are one with the Angels, just like an Angel; and when they descend from there to the middle dwelling, they are there as one with men, like a human Angel; and when they descend further from this, they are one with the guardian spirits <note>original: "geniis"</note> like a man of the world, and they instruct, reprove, and tame them. ### 397. I. On the WILL & INTELLECT.
,, 1. There are two Faculties in a person which 
,, make up their life: one is called the Will and the other the Intellect; they 
,, are distinct from each other, but so created that they may be one; and when

,, therefore, these are the human Mind, and all the life of a person is there in its beginnings, and from 
,, there in the body. 2. Just as all things in the Universe which are according to Order 
,, relate themselves to Good and Truth, so all things in a person relate to the Will and 
,, Intellect; for Good in a person belongs to their Will, and Truth in them 
,, belongs to their Intellect; for these two Faculties, or these two Lives of a person, 
,, are the receptacles and subjects of those things: the Will is the receptacle and subject 
,, of all Good, and the Intellect is the receptacle and subject of all Truth; 
,, Goods and Truths in a person are nowhere else; and because Goods and Truths 
,, in a person are nowhere else, therefore neither Love nor Faith are elsewhere, 
,, since Love is of good and Good is of love, and Faith is of truth and Truth 
,, is of faith. 3. The Will and Intellect also 
,, make up the Spirit of a person; for their Wisdom and Intelligence, and also their

This is especially necessary for a person of the Church, for just as all things of Heaven refer themselves to Good and Truth, so also do all things of the Church, because the good and truth of Heaven are also the good and truth of the Church. 3. It is according to <term>Divine Order<note>The inherent structure and laws by which God governs the universe</note></term> that Good and Truth be joined, and not separated, so that they are one and not two; for they proceed joined from God, and they are joined in Heaven, and therefore they shall be joined in the Church. The joining of good and truth is called in Heaven the <term>Heavenly Marriage<note>original: "Conjugium cæleste"</note></term>, for all who are there are in this Marriage. This is why, in the <term>Word<note>A reference to the Sacred Scriptures</note></term>, Heaven is compared to a Marriage, and why the Lord is called the Bridegroom and Husband, while Heaven is called the Bride and Wife; the Church is spoken of similarly. That Heaven and the Church are so called is because those who are there receive Divine Good within Truths. 4. All intelligence and wisdom which the Angels possess is from that Marriage, and not any from Good separated from Truth, nor from Truth separated from Good: it is the same for the people of the Church. 5. Since the joining of good and truth is like a marriage, it is clear that Good loves Truth, and in turn, Truth loves Good, and that each desires to be joined with the other. A person of the Church who does not have such love and such desire is not in the Heavenly Marriage, and thus the Church is not yet in them, since the joining of good and truth makes the Church. 6. Goods are manifold; in general, there is spiritual Good and natural Good, and both are joined in genuine moral Good. As there are Goods, so there are Truths; because Truths belong to Good, and are the forms of good. 7. As it is with Good and Truth, so it is—in the opposite way—with Evil and Falsity. For just as all things in the Universe that are according to Divine Order refer to Good and Truth, so all things that are against Divine Order refer to Evil and Falsity. Furthermore, just as Good loves to be joined to Truth, so Evil loves to be joined to Falsity, and vice versa; and just as all Intelligence and Wisdom are born from the union of good and truth, so all Insanity and Folly are born from the union of evil and falsity. The union of evil and falsity, viewed interiorly, is not a Marriage, but <term>Adultery<note>Used here in a spiritual sense to mean the perversion or corruption of what is sacred</note></term>. 8. From the fact that Evil and Falsity are opposites to Good and Truth, it is clear that Truth cannot be joined to Evil, nor Good to the Falsity of evil; if Truth is attached to Evil, it is no longer Truth, but Falsity, because it has been falsified; and if Good is attached to the Falsity of evil, it is no longer Good, but Evil, because it has been adulterated. However, Falsity that is not from evil <note>meaning an error made in ignorance rather than out of a desire to do harm</note> can be joined to Good. 9. No one who is in Evil and its resulting Falsity by conviction and life can know what Good and Truth are, since they believe their Evil to be Good, and thus believe their Falsity to be Truth; but everyone who is in Good and its resulting Truth by conviction and life can know what evil and falsity are. The reason is that all Good and its Truth is in its essence Heavenly, while all Evil and its resulting Falsity is in its essence Infernal; and everything Heavenly is in the light, and everything Infernal is in darkness.

### 399. III. ON LOVE IN GENERAL.

1. The very Life of a person is their Love, and as the Love is, such is the Life—indeed, such is the whole person. But it is the <term>ruling or reigning love<note>original: "Amor dominans"; the primary motivation that directs all other choices</note></term> that makes the person. This Love has many subordinate loves under it, which are its derivatives; these appear under a different outward appearance, but each of them is still present in the ruling Love, and with it they form one Kingdom. The Ruling Love is like their King and Head; it directs them, and through them—as through intermediate ends—it regards and intends its own Purpose, which is the primary and final goal of all things, both directly and indirectly. 2. That which belongs to the ruling love is what is loved above all things. What a person loves above all things is constantly present in their thought, because it is in their <term>Will<note>original: "Voluntas"; the seat of intention and desire</note></term>, and it constitutes their very Life. For example, one who loves riches above all things, whether money or possessions, is continually turning over in their mind how to acquire them; they rejoice deeply when they acquire them, they grieve deeply when they lose them; their heart is in them. One who loves Self above all things, treats themselves...

It is in his **Will** like a hidden vein of a river, which draws and carries him away even when he is doing something else, for it is that which gives him life. This is what one person explores in another and also perceives, and by it either leads him or acts with him. 4. A person is exactly as the **Ruling Principle** of his life is; by this he is distinguished from others. According to this, his **Heaven** is formed if he is good, and his **Hell** is formed if he is evil. However, what he thinks but does not love, he may also call delightful, but it is not the delight of his life. The delight of love is what is **Good** to a person, and the lack of delight is what is **Evil** to him. 6. There are two Loves from which all goods and truths exist, as if from their own fountains; and there are two Loves from which all evils and falsities exist. The two Loves from which all goods and truths exist are **Love for the Lord** and **Love toward the neighbor**; but the two Loves from which all evils and falsities exist are **Love of self** and **Love of the world**. When these two loves dominate, they are completely opposite to those former two Loves. 7. The two Loves which, as was said, are Love for the Lord and Love toward the neighbor, make **Heaven** within a person, for they reign in Heaven; and because they make Heaven within a person, they also make the **Church** within him. The two Loves from which all evils and falsities flow, which are Love of self and Love of the world, make **Hell** within a person, for they reign in Hell; consequently, they also destroy the Church within him. 8. The two Loves from which all goods and truths flow, which are the Loves of Heaven, open and form the **Internal spiritual man**, because they reside there; however, the two Loves from which all evils and falsities flow, the Loves of Hell, when they dominate, close and destroy the Internal spiritual man, and cause the person to become **Natural** and **Sensual** <note>In this system, "sensual" refers to the lowest level of human thought, tied strictly to the physical senses and worldly desires</note> according to the extent and quality of their dominion.

### 400. IV. ON LOVE OF SELF AND LOVE OF THE WORLD IN PARTICULAR.

> 1. **Love of self** is wishing well to oneself alone, and not to others except for the sake of oneself—not even to the Church, the Fatherland, any human society, or a fellow citizen. It is also doing good to them only for the sake of one's own reputation, honor, and glory; unless he sees these in the goods he does for them, he says in his heart: "What does it matter? Why do this? And what is in it for me?" and so he leaves it aside. From this it is clear that he who is in the love of self does not love the Church, nor the Fatherland, nor society, nor his fellow citizen, nor any truly Good thing, but **Only himself and his own**. 2. A person is in the **Love of self** when, in those things which he thinks and does, he does not regard the neighbor, nor the public, much less the Lord, but only himself and his own; consequently, when he does everything for the sake of himself and his own, and if he does it for the sake of the Public, it is only that it may be seen, and if for the neighbor, it is that he may favor himself. 3. It is said "for the sake of himself and his own," for he who loves himself also loves his own, who are specifically his children and grandchildren, and in general all who make one with him, whom he calls "his own." To love both the former and the latter is also to love himself, for he regards them as if in himself, and himself in them. Among those whom he calls "his own" are also all who praise, honor, and worship him. The rest he regards with the eyes of the body as people, but with the eyes of his spirit he regards them as little more than <term>phantoms<note>original: "larvas"; literally "masks" or "ghosts." It suggests that he does not see other people as real, living individuals with their own worth</note></term>. 4. That person is in the **Love of self** who despises his neighbor in comparison with himself; who treats him as an enemy if he does not favor him, and if he does not revere and worship him. He is even more in the love of self who, for that reason, hates and persecutes his neighbor; and still more so, he who burns with revenge against him and desires his destruction. Such people finally love to be cruel. 5. From a comparison with...

## 401. V. ON THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL MAN.

,, 1. Man was so created that he 
,, might be simultaneously in the spiritual World and in the natural World: the spiritual World 
,, is where the Angels are, and the natural World is where men are; and because man was so 
,, created, therefore an Internal and an External were given to him; an Internal, through 
,, which he might be in the spiritual World, and an External, through which he might be in 
,, the natural World. His Internal is what is called the <term>Internal man</term>, and the 
,, External is what is called the <term>External man</term>. 2. Every single person has an 
,, Internal and an External, but it is one way with the good, and another way with the 
,, evil; the Internal with the good is in Heaven and its light, and the External is in the 
,, World and its light, and this Light with them is illuminated by the light of Heaven, and 
,, so with them the Internal and the External act as one, like cause and effect, or like 
,, what is prior and what is posterior. But with the evil, the Internal is in Hell, and in its 
,, light, which light is darkness relative to the light of Heaven, and their External can 
,, be in a light similar to that in which the good are; therefore it is inverted: hence it is 
,, that the evil can speak and teach about faith, about charity, and about God, but not 
,, from faith, charity, and God, as the good do. 3. The <term>Internal man</term> is he who is 
,, called the <term>Spiritual man</term>, because he is in the Light of Heaven, which light is 
,, spiritual, and the <term>External man</term> is he who is called the <term>natural man</term>, 
,, because he is in the Light of the World, which light is natural: a person whose 
,, Internal is in the Light of Heaven, and whose External is in the light of the World, is 
,, a spiritual person in respect to both, because spiritual light from the interior illuminates 
,, the natural light, and makes the latter its own: but it is the reverse with the evil. 
,, 4. The <term>Internal spiritual man</term> viewed in himself is an Angel of Heaven, and 
,, also while he lives in the body, he is in society with Angels, although he does not 
,, know it, and after release from the body, he comes among the Angels; but the 
,, Internal man with the evil is <term>Satan</term>, and while he lives in the body, he is in 
,, society with them, and also after release from the body, he comes among them. 
,, 5. The interiors of the mind with those who are spiritual men are actually elevated 
,, toward Heaven, for they look to it primarily; but the interiors of the mind with those 
,, who are merely natural are turned away from Heaven and turned toward the 
,, World, because they look to the latter primarily. 6. Those who entertain only a

,, when a person thinks and wills well regarding the Lord and those things which are the Lord's, and when they think well of the neighbor and those things which are the neighbor’s, then they think and will from the **Spiritual Internal**, because they act from the faith of truth and the love of good. But when a person thinks and wills evilly regarding them, then they think and will from the **Infernal Internal** <note>original: "Interno infernali"; referring to the part of the human spirit that is connected to hellish influences</note>, because they act from the faith of what is false and the love of what is evil. In a word, to the extent that a person is in love toward the Lord and in love toward the neighbor, they are in the Spiritual Internal, and think, will, speak, and act from it. Thus it has been provided and ordered by the Lord that to the extent that a person thinks and wills from Heaven, the **Spiritual Man** is opened and formed; this opening is toward Heaven, even unto the Lord, and the formation is according to those things that belong to Heaven. Conversely, however, to the extent that a person thinks and wills not from Heaven but from the World, the Spiritual Internal man is closed, and the External is opened and formed; this opening is toward the World, and the formation is according to those things that belong to Hell. 8. Those in whom the Spiritual Internal man is opened into Heaven to the Lord are in the light of Heaven and in illumination from the Lord, and from this they have intelligence and wisdom; these see truth by the light of truth and perceive good from the love of good. But those in whom the Spiritual Internal man is closed do not know what the Internal man is, nor do they believe the Word, nor life after death, nor the things belonging to Heaven and the Church; and because they are only in **natural light** <note>original: "lumine naturali"; human reason unaided by spiritual revelation</note>, they believe Nature exists of itself and not from God; they see falsehood as truth and perceive evil as good. 9. The Internal and External being discussed are the Internal and External of the human Spirit; the Body is merely an added External within which these exist; for the body does nothing of itself, but acts from the spirit within it. It should be known that the Spirit of a person, after being released from the body, thinks, wills, speaks, and acts just as before; thinking and willing are then its Internal, while speaking and acting are its External.

# 402. VI. ON THE MERELY NATURAL AND SENSUAL MAN.

,, Since few know who are meant by **Sensual men** <note>In Swedenborg’s terminology, "sensual" refers to those who trust only their physical senses (sight, touch, etc.) rather than spiritual intuition or reason</note>, and what they are like, and yet it is important to know, they shall be described. 1. A "Sensual man" is one who judges everything from the Senses of the body, and who believes nothing except what he can see with his eyes and touch with his hands, saying that these things are something, and rejecting everything else; therefore, the sensual man is the lowest kind of natural man. 2. The interiors of his mind, which see by the light of Heaven, are closed, so that he sees nothing of the truth belonging to Heaven and the Church, because he thinks only in extremes <note>That is, at the surface level of physical reality</note> and not inwardly from any spiritual light. 3. And because he is in "thick" natural light, he is inwardly opposed to those things which belong to Heaven and the Church, and yet he can outwardly speak in favor of them, and even do so ardently if it serves his desire for power. 4. Sensual men reason sharply and skillfully because their thought is so close to their speech that it is almost in it, as if on their lips; and because they place all intelligence in speaking from memory alone. 5. Some of them can confirm whatever they wish, especially falsehoods, and after confirming them, they believe them to be true; they reason and confirm from the fallacies of the senses, by which the common people are captivated and persuaded. 6. Sensual men are more cunning and malicious than others. 7. The interiors of their minds are foul and filthy, since through them they communicate with the Hells. 8. Those who are in the Hells are sensual, and more so the deeper they are; the sphere of hellish spirits joins itself with the sensual aspects of a person from behind. 9. Since sensual men do not see any genuine truth in the light, but reason and argue about everything as to whether it is so, and these arguments are heard outside of them like the **gnashing of teeth** <note>original: "stridorem dentium"; a biblical reference to the state of those in spiritual darkness</note>, which in themselves are the collisions of falsehoods with each other, and also of the false and the true; it is thus clear what is signified by the "gnashing of teeth" in the Word. The reason is that reasoning from the fallacies of the senses corresponds to the teeth. 10. ## *That those three Loves, when rightly subordinated, perfect a human being, but when not rightly subordinated, they pervert and invert him.*

403. First, something will be said about the Subordination of those three Universal Loves, which are the Love of Heaven, the Love of the World, and the Love of self; and afterward about the influx and insertion of one into the other, and finally about the state of a person according to that subordination. These three Loves among themselves are like the three regions of the body: the highest of which is the Head, the middle is the Chest with the Belly, and the third is made of the Knees, Feet, and Soles. When the Love of Heaven makes the Head, the Love of the world the chest with the belly, and the love of self the feet with the soles, then the person is in a perfect state according to creation; for then the two lower Loves serve the highest, just as the Body and all its parts serve the Head. Therefore, when the Love of Heaven makes the Head, it flows into the Love of the World (which is principally the Love of wealth) and through this performs <term>uses: meaningful services or beneficial actions</term>; and mediately through this into the Love of self (which is principally the love of dignities <note>high rank or social status</note>) and through these performs uses; thus those three Loves breathe forth uses by the influx of one into another. Who does not understand that while a person, from Spiritual Love (which is from the Lord and is what is meant by the Love of Heaven), wills to perform uses, the Natural man performs them through wealth and his other goods, and the Sensual man in his own function, and that his honor consists in producing them? Who also does not understand that all works which a person performs with the body are done according to the state of his mind in the Head, and that if the Mind is in the Love of uses, the Body...

...the body <note>The word "pus" at the top of the page completes "corpus" (body) from the preceding page.</note> through its members may effect these things. This occurs because the **Will** and **Understanding** are in their origins in the Head, and in their derived effects in the Body—just as the will is present in deeds and thought is present in speech. By way of comparison, it is like the prolific power of a seed present in each and every part of a tree, through which it produces fruits, which are its uses. It is also like the fire and light inside a crystalline vessel, which is warmed and made transparent by them. Furthermore, the spiritual sight in the Mind, combined with the natural sight in the body—in a person in whom those three loves are justly and rightly subordinated—can be compared to an African Apple <note>original: "Pomo Africano"; likely a pomegranate or a citrus fruit, which Swedenborg uses as a metaphor for spiritual transparency</note> which is translucent all the way to the center where the seed-case is located. Something similar is meant by these words of the Lord: *The lamp of the body is the eye; if the eye is simple <note>or "clear/sound"</note>, that is, if it is good, the whole body is full of light.* Matthew 6:22; Luke 11:34. No person of sound reason can condemn wealth, for in the common Body [of society] it is like blood in a human being; nor can one condemn the honors attached to public offices, for they are the hands of the King and the pillars of Society, provided that the natural and sensual loves of these things are subordinated to spiritual love. There are even administrative offices in Heaven, and dignities attached to them, but those who perform them love nothing more than performing uses, because they are spiritual.

**404.** But a person takes on an entirely different state if the **Love of the World** (or of wealth) forms the Head—that is, if it is the reigning love. For then the **Love of Heaven** is exiled from the Head and moves into the Body. A person in this state prefers the World over Heaven; they may indeed worship God, but they do so from a purely natural love which places merit <note>the belief that one earns salvation through their own deeds</note> in all worship. They also do good to their neighbor, but only for the sake of rewards. To these people, the things of Heaven are like veils in which they walk about appearing radiant to the eyes of men, but dark to the eyes of Angels; for when the Love of the World possesses the Internal man and the Love of Heaven the External, the former obscures all things of the Church and hides them as if under a veil. Truly, this love exists in great variety: it is worse to the degree it verges toward avarice, in which the Love of Heaven turns black. Similarly if it verges toward pride and eminence over others from self-love. It is different, however, if it verges toward extravagance. It is less harmful if its goal is splendid palaces, decorations, magnificent clothing, retinues of servants, horses and carriages for display, and other such things. The quality of any Love is judged by the end <note>the goal or purpose</note> which it regards and intends. This Love can be compared to a blackish crystal that suffocates the light and only varies it into gloomy and fading colors. It is also like a mist or clouds that take away the sun's rays. It is also like the must of unfermented wine <note>unrefined grape juice</note>, which tastes sweet but upsets the stomach. Such a person, viewed from Heaven, appears like a hunchbacked man walking with a bowed head looking at the ground; when he raises his head toward Heaven, he twists his muscles and quickly falls back into his prone position. These people were called <note>original: "Mammones"</note> Mammons by the Ancients in the Church, and <note>original: "Plutones"</note> Plutos by the Greeks.

**405.** If, however, the **Love of Self** (or the Love of Ruling) forms the head, then the **Love of Heaven** passes through the body to the feet. As that love increases, the Love of Heaven descends through the ankles to the soles of the feet, and if it increases further, it passes into the shoes and is trampled underfoot. There is a Love of Ruling that comes from Love of the Neighbor, and a Love of Ruling that comes from Love of Self. Those who are in the Love of Ruling from Love of the Neighbor seek dominion for the sake of an end, so that they may perform uses for the Public and for individuals; for this reason, dominion is also entrusted to them in the Heavens. Emperors, Kings, and Commanders who were born and educated for dominion—if they humble themselves before God—are sometimes less in that [selfish] love than those of low birth who seek eminent ranks over others out of pride. But to those who are in the Love of Ruling from the love of self, the Love of Heaven is like a footstool upon which they place their feet for the sake of the common people, yet when the public is not watching, they throw it into a corner or out the door. The reason is that they love themselves alone, and consequently they immerse the wills and thoughts of their minds in their <term>Proprium</term> <note>a technical term for the "Selfhood" or that which is one's own, which Swedenborg describes as being inherently inclined toward evil</note>, which in itself is hereditary evil; and this is diametrically opposed to the Love of Heaven. The evils belonging to those who are in the Love of Ruling from self-love are generally these: Con-

Since the Love of Heaven holds the highest place in a perfected person and acts as the Head for the others that follow, and the Love of the World is below it and is like the chest beneath the head, and the Love of Self is below this like the feet, it follows that if this Love of Self were to make itself the Head, it would completely invert the person. In that case, in the presence of Angels, he would appear as if lying bent over with his head toward the ground and his back toward heaven; and when he is at worship, he would appear to be jumping on his hands and feet like a panther cub <note>original: "pullus pantherae"; Swedenborg often uses animalistic imagery to describe the spiritual appearance of those who have rejected divine order</note>. Furthermore, he would appear in various forms of beasts with two Heads: one above with a wild animal's face, and another below with a human face, which would be continually pushed down by the upper one and forced to look at the ground. All these are Sensual men <term>Sensual men: individuals who judge everything solely by their physical senses and whose thoughts are buried in the material world</term>, and are such as were described above in article 402.

### ### That every individual person is the Neighbor who must be loved, but according to the quality of his good.

406. Man is not born for his own sake, but for the sake of others—that is, so that he does not live for himself alone but for others. Otherwise, there would be no cohesive Society, and no good within it. It is a common saying that "everyone is his own neighbor," but the Doctrine of Charity teaches how this should be understood: namely, that each person should provide for the necessities of his own life, such as food, clothing, habitation, and other things which are necessarily required in the civil life in which he exists. This is not only for himself, but also for his own family; and not just for the present time, but also for the future. For unless one procures for himself the necessities of life, he is not in a state to practice Charity, for he would be in a state of universal want. 

How each person ought to be a Neighbor to himself can be seen from this comparison: everyone must provide for his body with food; this comes first, but for the end that there may be a healthy Mind in a healthy Body <note>original: "Mens sana in Corpore sano"</note>. And everyone must provide for his Mind with its own food, namely, such things as belong to intelligence and judgment, but for the end that he may thereby be in a state to serve a fellow citizen, society, the fatherland, the Church, and thus the Lord. He who does this provides well for himself for eternity. From this it is clear what is first in time, and what is first in the intended goal; and that which is first in the intended goal is that toward which all things look. It is just like someone building a House: first he lays the foundation, but the foundation is for the house, and the house is for habitation. He who believes he is the Neighbor in the first place or primarily is like one who regards the foundation as the goal, not the habitation; yet the habitation itself is the first and final goal, and the House with its foundation is merely the means to that end.

407. What it means to love the Neighbor shall now be stated. To love the neighbor is not only to wish and do good to a relative, friend, and a good person, but also to a stranger, an enemy, and an evil person. However, Charity is practiced toward these different people in different ways: toward a relative and friend it is done through direct benefits; but toward an enemy and an evil person it is done through indirect benefits, which are accomplished through exhortations, discipline, and punishments, and thus corrections. This can be illustrated thus: A Judge who, according to law and justice, punishes a wrongdoer, loves his neighbor, for in this way he corrects him and looks out for the citizens, lest the wrongdoer harm them. Everyone knows that a Father who punishes his children when they do wrong loves them; conversely, he who does not punish them for that reason loves their evils, which cannot be called Charity. Furthermore, if someone repels an attacking enemy and, for the sake of safe...

...strikes with weapons, or hands him over to a judge so that he may avert harm from himself, yet with the intention that he might eventually become his friend, that person acts from the vein of Charity. Even wars that have the goal of protecting the Fatherland and the Church are not against Charity; the purpose for the sake of which a thing is done declares whether it is Charity or not.

408. Since, therefore, Charity in its origin is "willing well" <term>bene velle; the internal act of benevolence</term>, and willing well resides in the **Internal man**, it is clear that when someone who possesses Charity resists an enemy, punishes a guilty person, or corrects the wicked, he does this by means of the **External man**. For this reason, after he has performed the action, he returns to the Charity which is in his Internal man; then, as much as he can and as much as it is helpful, he wills well to that person, and from that goodwill, he does good to him. Those who possess genuine Charity have a **Zeal** for what is good. That Zeal in the External man can appear like anger and a flaming fire, but it is extinguished and calmed as soon as the adversary repents. It is different for those who have no Charity; their Zeal is actually anger and hatred, for their Internal man seethes and takes fire from these passions.

409. Before the Lord came into the World, hardly anyone knew what the Internal man was, or what Charity was; for this reason, He taught Love (that is, Charity) in so many places. This constitutes the distinction between the **Old Testament** (or Covenant) and the **New**. The Lord taught that an Adversary and an Enemy must be treated with kindness out of Charity, as seen in Matthew: *“You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,’ but I say to you, Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who hurt and persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in Heaven”* (Chapter 5: 43, 44, 45). And to Peter, who asked how many times he should forgive someone sinning against him, *“whether up to seven times?”* the Lord responded, *“I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven”* (Matthew 18: 21, 22). I have also heard from Heaven that the Lord forgives everyone their sins and never takes vengeance—He does not even impute them to the person, because He is Love itself and Good itself—but nevertheless, sins are not wiped away by this alone, for they are not wiped away except through repentance. For if He told Peter to forgive up to seventy times seven, what would the Lord Himself not do?

410. Since Charity itself resides in the Internal man (where the goodwill is) and flows from there into the External man (where the good deed is), it follows that the Internal man is the one to be loved, and the External man because of him. Therefore, a person is to be loved according to the quality of the good that is within him. For this reason, **Good itself** is essentially the **Neighbor**. This can be illustrated by this example: when someone chooses a house manager or a servant from three or four candidates, does he not investigate his "Internal man" and choose the one who is sincere and faithful, and love him for those qualities? Similarly, a King or Magistrate chooses a person capable of a specific function from several candidates and rejects the incapable one, no matter what kind of face he puts on, or how much he speaks and acts to gain favor. Since every person is a neighbor, and there is an infinite variety of people, and each is to be loved as a neighbor according to his specific good, it is clear that there are types and species, as well as degrees of Love toward the neighbor. Now, because the Lord is to be loved above all things, it follows that the degrees of that love are to be measured according to Love for Him—that is, how much of the Lord (or how much from the Lord) another person possesses within himself. For a person possesses exactly that much good, because all good is from the Lord. But because these degrees are in the Internal man, and the Internal rarely manifests itself clearly in the World, it is sufficient that the Neighbor be loved according to the degrees one can recognize. However, these degrees are clearly perceived after death; there, the affections of the will and the resulting thoughts of the understanding create a "spiritual sphere" around people, which is felt in various ways. In this world, that spiritual sphere is absorbed by the material Body and encloses itself within the natural sphere that flows out from a person. That there are degrees of Love toward the neighbor is evident from the Lord’s **Parable of the Samaritan**, who showed mercy to the man wounded by robbers, whom the Priest and the Levite passed by. When the Lord asked which of those three seemed to have been the Neighbor, the reply was, *“the one who showed mercy”* (Luke 10: 30–37).

411. It is written, *You shall love the Lord your God above all things, and your neighbor as yourself,* Luke 10:27. To love the neighbor as oneself is not to despise him in comparison to oneself, but to act justly with him, and not to pass an evil judgment upon him. The Law of Charity, brought and given by the Lord Himself, is this: *Whatever you would want men to do to you, so also do you to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets,* Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31.

32. <note>The original text numbers this paragraph as 32, though it follows 411; it serves as a sub-point on the quality of love.</note> Those who are in the **Love of Heaven** love the neighbor in this way; but those who are in the **Love of the World** love the neighbor from the world and for the sake of the world; and those who are in the **Love of Self** love the neighbor from themselves and for the sake of themselves.

## That Man in the plural, which is a Society smaller or larger, and that Man in the composite of these, which is the Country, is the Neighbor who must be loved.

412. Those who do not know what the <term>Neighbor (Proximus)</term> is in the genuine sense imagine that it is nothing other than a human being in the singular, and that providing benefits to such a person is loving the neighbor. But the neighbor and love toward him extend more broadly; indeed, it ascends as the number of humans is multiplied. Who cannot understand that loving many people in a gathering is a greater love of the neighbor than loving one single individual from that gathering? The reason why a Society, whether smaller or larger, is the Neighbor, is because a society is "man in the plural." From this it follows that he who loves a Society loves those of whom the Society consists; therefore, he who wills well and does well to a Society consults the interests of every individual in it. 

A Society is like a single man; even those who enter into it compose it as if it were a single Body, and they are distinguished among themselves like members in a single body. When the Lord, and the Angels from Him, look down upon the earth, they see an entire Society no differently than as a single man, and its form is seen based on the qualities of those within it. It was even granted to me to see a certain Society in Heaven exactly as a single man, in a stature similar to that of a man in the World. 

That a fuller love toward the neighbor is love toward a Society rather than toward a separate or individual person manifests itself in the fact that <term>Dignities (high offices)</term> are distributed according to the leadership over Societies, and honors are given to them according to the <term>Uses (useful services)</term> they perform. For there are Offices in the world, higher and lower, in subordination according to a more or less universal government over Societies; and he is a King whose government is the most universal. To each person, according to the breadth of his duty and the good of the uses he performs, there is a reward, glory, and common love. 

But the <term>Governors (Moderatores)</term> of this world can perform uses and consult the interests of a Society and yet not love the neighbor—as do those who perform uses and consult the interests of others for the sake of the World and for the sake of themselves, so that they may appear great or deserve to be raised to higher dignities. These people, although they are not distinguished as such in the World, are nevertheless distinguished in Heaven. Therefore, those who had performed uses out of Love for the neighbor are also placed as Governors over heavenly Societies, and there they are in splendor and honor; yet they do not set their heart on these honors, but on the uses. Others, however, who performed uses out of Love for the World and of self, are rejected.

413. The distinction between love toward the neighbor and its exercise toward a man in the singular versus a man in the plural (or a Society) is like the difference between the duty of a citizen, the duty of a magistrate, and the duty of a general. It is also like the difference between the one who traded with two **Talents** and the one who traded with ten (Matthew 25:14 to 31). It is a difference like the value of a <term>shekel (sicli)</term> and the value of a talent; or between the use of the fruit from a single vine and from a whole vineyard, or from an olive tree and an olive grove, or from a single tree and a whole garden. Love toward the neighbor also ascends more and more interiorly within a person; and as it ascends, he loves a Society more than an individual person, and his <term>Country (Patria)</term> more than a Society. Now, since Charity consists of willing well and therefrom doing well, it follows that it is practiced in almost the same way—

...must be practiced toward a Society as toward an individual man; but it is practiced differently toward a Society of good people than toward a Society of evil people. Toward the latter, Charity must be practiced according to natural equity, but toward the former according to spiritual equity; but concerning these two forms of equity, we shall see elsewhere.

414. That the Country <note>original: *Patria*; literally "fatherland," referring to the nation or political community</note> is the Neighbor in preference to a Society is because the country consists of many societies, and therefore Love toward it is a more extensive and higher love. Furthermore, to love one's country is to love the public welfare. The reason the Country is the Neighbor is because it is like a Parent; for a person was born there, it has nourished and continues to nourish him, and it has protected and continues to protect him from injuries. One must do good to the Country out of Love according to its necessities, some of which are natural and some spiritual. Natural necessities regard civil life and order, and Spiritual ones regard spiritual life and order. That the Country must be loved—not as a man loves himself, but above himself—is a Law inscribed on human Hearts. From this law comes the principle declared by every just man: that if destruction threatens the country from an enemy or elsewhere, it is noble to die for it, and glorious for a soldier to shed his blood for it. This is said because the country is to be loved to such an extent. It should be known that those who love their Country and do good to it from goodwill, after death love the Lord’s Kingdom, for there, the Kingdom is the "Country"; and those who love the Lord’s Kingdom love the Lord, because the Lord is everything in all things of His Kingdom.

### *That the Church is the Neighbor who is to be loved in a higher degree, and the Lord’s Kingdom in the highest.*

415. Since man is born for eternal life and is introduced into this through the Church, the Church is therefore to be loved as the Neighbor in a higher degree. This is because she teaches the means that lead to eternal life and introduces one into it; she leads to it through the truths of doctrine and introduces through the goods of life <note>In this context, "goods of life" refers to living according to moral and spiritual principles</note>. This does not mean that the Priesthood <note>original: *Sacerdotium*</note> is to be loved in a higher degree and the Church because of it, but rather that the good and truth of the Church are to be loved, and the Priesthood on account of these; in this way the priesthood serves, and it is to be honored according to the degree that it serves. The reason the Church is the Neighbor to be loved in a higher degree—and thus even above the Country—is also because man is initiated into Civil Life by his Country, but into spiritual Life by the Church; and it is this spiritual life that distinguishes man from a merely animal life. Moreover, civil life is temporary and comes to an end, and then it is as though it had never been; but Spiritual life, because it has no end, is eternal. Therefore, "Being" <note>original: *Esse*; the state of true existence</note> can be predicated of the latter, and "non-being" of the former. The difference is as between the finite and the infinite, between which no comparison can be made; for the eternal is infinite in respect to time.

416. The reason the Lord’s Kingdom is the Neighbor to be loved in the highest degree is because by the Lord’s Kingdom is meant the Church throughout the whole World—which is called the Communion of Saints—and it also refers to Heaven. Therefore, he who loves the Lord’s Kingdom loves all those in the entire World who acknowledge the Lord and have faith in Him and Charity toward the neighbor; and he also loves all in Heaven. Those who love the Lord’s Kingdom love the Lord above all things, and consequently they possess Love to God above all others; for the Church in the Heavens and on Earth is the Body of the Lord, for they are in the Lord and the Lord in them. Thus, Love toward the Lord’s Kingdom is Love toward the neighbor in its fullness; for those who love the Lord’s Kingdom not only love the Lord above all things, but also love the neighbor as themselves. For Love to the Lord is a universal Love, and is therefore present in each and every thing of spiritual Life, and also in each and every thing of natural Life. Indeed, that love resides in the highest parts of a person, and these highest things flow into the lower ones and give them life—just as the Will flows into all things of intention and then into action, and...

It emphasizes that spiritual life and the eternal kingdom take precedence over civil life and temporal nations.</summary>

...the Understanding into everything of thought and thereafter of speech: wherefore the Lord says, *Seek first the Kingdom of the Heavens and its Justice, then all things will be added to you*, Matthew 6:33. That the Kingdom of the Heavens is the Lord's Kingdom is clear from these words in Daniel: *Behold, with the clouds of the Heavens, like the* SON OF MAN <note>original: *FILIUS HOMINIS*; a messianic title used by Daniel and Jesus to describe the divine-human nature</note>, *one was coming; and to Him was given Dominion, Glory, and a Kingdom, and all Peoples, Nations, and Tongues shall worship Him; His Dominion is an everlasting dominion which shall not pass away, and His Kingdom one that shall not perish*, Chapter 7: 13, 14.

## *That loving the Neighbor, viewed in itself, is not loving the Person, but the Good that is in the Person.*

417. Who does not know that a human is not a human because of a human face and a human body, but because of the wisdom of his Understanding and the goodness of his Will? As the quality of these rises, it makes him more of a human. When a human is born, he is more of a brute than any animal, but he becomes human through instructions, which, as they are received, form his Mind, from which and according to which a human is a human. There are beasts whose faces resemble human faces, but they enjoy no faculty of understanding or of doing anything from the understanding; rather, they act from instinct, which their natural love excites. The difference is that a beast sounds out the affections of its love, but a human speaks those affections as they are brought into thought; also, that a beast looks at the earth with a downward gaze, while a human looks at Heaven in every direction with an upright face. From these things it can be concluded that a human becomes a human only so far as he speaks from sound reason and regards his dwelling-place in Heaven; and that he is not a human so far as he speaks from perverse reason and regards his dwelling-place only in the World. Yet these are still humans—not in act, but in potential—for every human enjoys the power of understanding truths and willing goods; but insofar as he does not wish to do goods and understand truths, he can only simulate a human in outward things and act as his ape <note>original: *simiam*; implies a mimic or someone imitating human behavior without genuine human substance</note>.

418. That Good is the Neighbor is because Good belongs to the will, and the Will is the Being <note>original: *Esse*; a philosophical term referring to the fundamental essence or "is-ness" of a thing</note> of a human's life. Truth of the Understanding is also the neighbor, but only insofar as it proceeds from the good of the will; for the good of the will forms itself in the understanding and there presents itself to be seen in the light of reason. That good is the neighbor is clear from all experience. Who loves a person except for the quality of his will and understanding—that is, from the good and just within him? For example: Who loves a King, Prince, General, Governor, Consul, any Magistrate, or any Judge, except for the Judgment from which they act and speak? Who loves a Primate, some Minister of the Church, or a Canon, except for his learning, integrity of life, and zeal for the salvation of souls? Who loves a General of an army or any officer under him, except for his courage joined with prudence? Who loves a Merchant except for his sincerity? Who loves a worker or a servant except for his faithfulness? Indeed, who loves a tree except for its fruit, the soil except for its fertility, a stone except for its value, and so on. And, what is remarkable, not only does an honest man love what is good and just in another, but even an evil man does, because with such a person he is in no fear of losing his reputation, honor, or wealth. But the love of good in an evil man is not Love of the neighbor, for an evil man does not inwardly love another except so far as that person serves him. But to love the good in another from the good in oneself is genuine love toward the neighbor, for then Goods kiss each other and join together.

419. The human who loves good because it is good, and truth because it is truth, loves the neighbor in an eminent way, for the reason that he loves the Lord, who is Good itself and Truth itself. From no other source is there a love of good and thence of truth, and thus of the neighbor; so is love toward the neighbor formed from a heavenly origin. Whether you say "use" <term>Use (usus): in this context, the practical application of goodness or the service one performs for others</term> or "good," it is the same thing; wherefore to do uses is to do goods, and according to the amount and quality of the use in the goods, such and so far are the goods truly good.

### *That Charity and Good Works are two distinct things, just as willing well and doing well are distinct.*

420. In every individual, there is an Internal and an External. The Internal is what is called the Internal man, and the External is what is called the External man. However, someone who does not know what the internal and external man are might believe that the internal man is the part that thinks and wills, and the external is the part that speaks and acts. While it is true that speaking and acting belong to the External man, and thinking and willing belong to the Internal, these do not essentially constitute the External and Internal man. In common perception, the human Mind is indeed the Internal man, but the Mind itself is divided into two regions: one region, which is higher and more interior, is spiritual; the other, which is lower and more exterior, is natural. 

The spiritual mind looks primarily into the spiritual world and takes as its objects those things found there, whether they are of Heaven or of Hell (for both are in the spiritual world). The natural mind, however, looks primarily into the natural world and takes as its objects those things found there, whether they be good or evil. Every action and speech of a human proceeds from the lower region of the mind directly, and from its higher region indirectly, because the lower region of the mind is closer to the bodily senses, while the higher region is more remote from them. This division of the mind exists in humans because they were created to be spiritual and natural at the same time, and thus a human and not a beast. 

From this it is clear that the person who looks primarily to the world and to themselves becomes an External man, because they are natural not only in body but also in mind. Conversely, the person who looks primarily to the things of Heaven and the Church is an Internal man, because they are spiritual in both mind and body. The reason they are spiritual in body as well is that actions and speech proceed from the higher mind (which is spiritual) through the lower mind (which is natural). For it is well known that effects proceed from the body, but the causes that produce them proceed from the mind, and the cause is everything within the effect. That the human mind is so divided is clearly evident from the fact that a person can act the part of a pretender, a flatterer, a hypocrite, or an actor <note>original: *histrionem*; a stage-player</note>; they can agree with another’s words and yet laugh at them in their heart. They do the latter from the higher mind, but the former from the lower.

421. From these things, it can be seen how we are to understand that Charity and Good Works are as distinct as willing well and doing well. Specifically, they are formally distinct, like the Mind that thinks and wills is distinct from the body through which the Mind speaks and acts. But they are also essentially distinct because the Mind itself is distinct; as stated above, its interior region is spiritual and its exterior is natural. Therefore, if works proceed from the spiritual mind, they proceed from its "willing well" <note>original: *bene velle*; the faculty of goodwill or intention</note>, which is Charity. If, however, they proceed from the natural mind, they proceed from a "willing well" that is not Charity, even though it may appear as Charity in its external form. Such an action is not Charity in its internal form; and Charity in external form alone may present the appearance of Charity, but it does not possess the essence of Charity. 

This can be illustrated by a comparison with seeds in the earth: from every seed there grows a shrub, either useful or useless, depending on the quality of the seed. Similarly, spiritual seed—which is the truth of the Church from the Word—forms Doctrine; this is useful if it comes from genuine truths, and useless if from falsified ones. In the same way, Charity comes from "willing well," whether that willing is for the sake of oneself and the world, or for the sake of the neighbor in the narrow or broad sense. If it is for the sake of oneself and the world, it is spurious Charity; but if it is for the sake of the neighbor, it is genuine Charity. But more on these matters may be seen in the Chapter on Faith, specifically in the Article where it is shown: *That Charity is willing well, and that Good Works are doing well from willing well, n. 473. And that Charity and Faith are only mental and fleeting things unless, when possible, they are determined into Works and coexist within them, n. 375, 376.* <note>These numbers refer to specific sections or "paragraphs" within Swedenborg’s published theological works.</note>

<summary>This page explains the psychological and spiritual distinction between internal intentions (Charity) and external actions (Good Works), defining the human mind as having both spiritual and natural regions.</summary>

## *That Charity itself is to act justly and faithfully in the office, business, and work in which each person is, and with whom they have any dealing.*

422. The reason why Charity itself consists in acting justly and faithfully in the office, business, and work in which a person is engaged, is because everything a person does in this way is useful to Society; and use is good, and good—in a sense abstracted from persons—is the neighbor. It was shown above that not only an individual human, but also a smaller society, and even one’s own country, is the neighbor. 

As an example: A **King** who leads his subjects by example in doing well, who wills that they live according to the laws of justice, rewards those who live so, regards everyone according to their merit, protects them against injuries and invasions, acts as the Father of the Kingdom, and looks to the common prosperity of his people—in his heart there is Charity, and his deeds are good works. A **Priest** <note>In Swedenborg’s time, this refers generally to ministers or clergy of the church.</note> who teaches truths from the Word, and through them leads to the good of life and thus to Heaven—because he looks to the souls of the people of his church—exercises Charity preeminently. A **Judge** who judges according to justice and the law, and not for the sake of a bribe, friendship, or family connection, looks to the welfare of society and the individual; to Society, because it is thereby kept in obedience to the law and in fear of transgressing it; and to the individual, because justice triumphs over injustice. A **Merchant**, if he acts from sincerity and not from fraud, looks to the welfare of the neighbor with whom he does business. It is the same for a workman or a craftsman, if he does his work rightly and sincerely, and not deceitfully or fallaciously. The same applies to all others, such as ship-masters and sailors, or farmers and servants.

423. The reason why this is Charity itself is because Charity can be defined as doing good to the neighbor daily and continually; not only to the neighbor in the singular, but to the neighbor in the plural. This cannot be done except through the good and the just in the office, business, and work in which each person is, and with those with whom they have any dealing; for a person does this every day, and even when not actively doing it, it continually resides in the mind and is what they think about and intend. 

The person who exercises Charity in this way becomes more and more a "form" of Charity; for justice and faithfulness form their mind, and the exercise of these forms their body, so that gradually, from their very form, they will and think nothing other than those things which belong to charity. These people eventually become like those of whom it is said in the Word <note>A reference to Jeremiah 31:33 and Hebrews 8:10 regarding the New Covenant.</note> that they have the Law written on their hearts. They also do not place merit <note>meaning they do not seek "spiritual credit" or a reward in heaven</note> in their works, because they do not think about merit, but about duty—that it is becoming of a citizen to act this way. But a person can by no means act from spiritual justice and faithfulness from themselves; for every person inherits from their parents a tendency to act justly and well for the sake of themselves and the world, and no one acts for the sake of the good and the just itself. Therefore, only he who worships the Lord, and acts from the Lord while acting as if from himself, acquires spiritual charity and becomes imbued with it through practice.

424. There are many who act justly and faithfully in their function, and although they thus perform works of Charity, they still do not possess any Charity within themselves. These are people in whom the love of self and the world predominates, and not the love of heaven; and if by chance heavenly love is present, it is beneath the other like a servant under his master, or like a common soldier under a commander, or like a doorkeeper standing at the gate.

---

425. A distinction must be made between the *duties* <term>officia: the functional responsibilities of one's job</term> of Charity and its *benefactions* <term>beneficia: voluntary acts of kindness or charity like almsgiving</term>. By the duties of Charity are meant the exercises of Charity which proceed immediately from...

...proceed, which, because they are primarily related to the function in which each person is engaged, was shown just above. However, by **Benefactions** <term>beneficia: acts of kindness, charity, or assistance performed outside of one's professional or daily duties</term> are understood those helps which are performed outside of those regular functions. They are called "benefactions" because it is within a person's freedom and choice to do them, and when they are done, they are seen by the recipient as nothing other than favors. These are distributed according to the reasons and intentions that the benefactor turns over in their mind. 

In the common faith, it is believed that **Charity** is nothing other than giving to the poor, helping the needy, caring for widows and orphans, contributing funds toward the building of hospitals, infirmaries, guest houses, and orphanages, and especially toward Churches <note>original: "Templa"; here referring to church buildings and religious institutions</note> and their decorations and endowments. But many of these are not specific to Charity itself, but are external to it. Those who place Charity itself in these benefactions alone cannot help but place **merit** <term>meritum: the belief that one earns or deserves salvation and a reward in heaven through their good deeds</term> in those works. And even if they might say with their mouth that they do not wish them to be seen as merits, nevertheless the faith in merit lies hidden within. 

This is clearly evident from such people after death: they then enumerate their works and demand salvation as a reward. But at that time, an inquiry is made into the origin of those works—and thus their quality. If it is found that they proceeded either from pride, or from a pursuit of reputation, or from mere munificence, or from friendship, or from a purely natural inclination, or from hypocrisy, then they are judged according to that origin, for the quality of the origin is within the works. 

However, **genuine Charity** proceeds from those who have imbued it through justice and judgment in the works they do, without the goal of remuneration, according to the Lord’s words in *Luke 14:12, 13, 14*. These people also call the things mentioned above "benefactions," as well as "duties," even though they are acts of Charity.

426. It is well known that some who have performed those Benefactions—which appear before the world like "images" of charity—imagine and believe that they have practiced Works of Charity. They look at them much like many in the Papacy look at **Indulgences** <note>In the Roman Catholic tradition of the time, these were often perceived as payments or acts to reduce the punishment for sins</note>, through which they are purified from sins and, like the regenerated, ought to be given Heaven. And yet, they still do not regard as sins their adulteries, hatreds, vengeances, frauds, and in general the lusts of the flesh, in which they indulge at will. But what then are those good works other than painted images of Angels in company with devils, or boxes of lapis lazuli containing hydras? 

But it is entirely different if those benefactions are done by those who flee the aforementioned evils as being hateful to Charity. Truly, those Benefactions are beneficial in many ways, especially giving to the poor and to beggars; for through them, boys, girls, servants, maids, and in general all simple-minded people, are initiated into Charity. These are its external forms through which they become accustomed to the duties of Charity; they are its rudiments, and at that stage, they are like unripe fruit. But with those who are afterwards perfected by right knowledge concerning Charity and Faith, they become like ripe fruit; and then they look back at those earlier works done from simplicity of heart as nothing other than duties.

427. The reason why those Benefactions are believed today to be the specific acts of Charity which are understood in the Word as "good works," is because Charity is often described in the Word by giving to the poor, bringing aid to the needy, and looking after widows and orphans. But it has been unknown until now that the Word in its literal sense names only such things as are external—even the most external parts of worship—and that spiritual things, which are internal, are understood through them. On this matter, see the chapter on **SACRED SCRIPTURE** (numbers 173 to 209), from which it is clear that by the "poor," "needy," "widows," and "orphans" named there, those specific people are not meant, but rather those who are such in a spiritual sense. That by the "poor" are meant those who are not in the knowledge of truth and good, see ***APOCALYPSE REVEALED*** <note>One of Swedenborg's major published works providing a spiritual interpretation of the Book of Revelation</note>, no. 209. That by "widows" are meant those who are without truths and yet desire truths (no. 764); and so forth.

428. Those who are naturally merciful from birth, but do not make their natural qualities spiritual—whereby they would act from genuine Charity—believe that Charity consists in giving to any poor person and helping any needy person. They do not first inquire whether that poor or needy person is good or evil; for they say that this is not necessary, since God looks only at the help and the alms. But these people after...

For those who performed them out of that blind idea of Charity then do good equally to the evil and the good; and the evil, through those gifts, perform evil deeds and thereby harm the good. Therefore, those benefactors are also a cause of the injury to the good. For to do good to an evildoer is like giving bread to the devil, which he turns into poison—for all bread in the hand of the devil is poison—and if it is not, he turns it into something that allows him to entice others to evil through these kind acts. It is like handing a sword to an enemy with which to kill someone; it is like giving a shepherd's staff to a man-wolf to lead the sheep to pasture, when instead, once he has it, he drives the sheep from the pastures into the wilderness and slaughters them there. It is like giving a governorship to a bandit, who only keeps his mind and eyes on the plunder, dispensing laws and making judgments according to the wealth and abundance of the loot.
