## *That there are Duties of Charity: some Public, some Domestic, and some Private.*

429. The Benefactions of Charity <term>beneficia: voluntary acts of kindness or charity outside of one's job</term> and the Duties of Charity <term>debita: things one is obligated to do out of necessity or moral law</term> are distinct from one another, just like those things done from free choice are distinct from those done out of necessity. Yet by "Duties of Charity" here, we do not mean the official duties of roles in the Kingdom or Republic—such as a minister's duty to minister, or a judge's duty to judge, and so on—but rather the duties of any person in whatever role they hold. Therefore, these duties have a different origin and flow from a different will; they are performed out of Charity by those who are in Charity, and conversely, out of no Charity by those who are not.

430. **PUBLIC DUTIES OF CHARITY** are primarily taxes and customs duties <note>original: "Tributa & Vectigalia"</note>, which are not to be confused with official job duties. These are paid with one heart by those who are spiritual, and another by those who are merely natural. Spiritual people pay them out of goodwill because they are collections for the preservation of the Country, and for the protection of it and the Church, as well as for the administration carried out by officers and officials whose salaries and stipends must be paid from the Public Treasury. Therefore, those for whom the Country and the Church are the Neighbor <note>in this context, "Neighbor" refers to the collective good or the community rather than just an individual</note> pay these out of a spontaneous and productive will, and they consider it a crime to deceive or avoid them. But those for whom the Country and Church are not the Neighbor perform them with a reluctant and resistant will; and whenever the opportunity is given, they defraud and steal from the system, for to these people, their own House and their own Flesh are the Neighbor.

431. **DOMESTIC DUTIES OF CHARITY** are those of a husband toward his wife, and a wife toward her husband; then of a father and mother toward their children, and children toward their father and mother; as well as those of a master and mistress toward their male and female servants, and theirs toward them. These Duties, because they concern upbringing and the management of a home, are so many that if they were listed, they would fill a book. Every person is led into these duties by a different love than into the duties of their profession. A husband’s toward his wife and a wife’s toward her husband come from marriage love <term>Amor conjugialis: the spiritual and natural love between a husband and wife</term> and according to it. A father’s and mother’s toward their children come from a love implanted in everyone, which is called natural parental affection <term>Storge</term>; and children’s toward their parents from another love and according to it, which joins itself closely with the obedience of duty. The duties of a master and mistress toward servants, however, are drawn from the love of ruling, and this from each person's state of mind. But marriage love and love toward children, with their duties and the exercise of those duties, do not produce love toward the neighbor in the same way as the exercise of duties in one's profession does. For the love called parental affection <note>original: "Storge"</note> is found among the evil just as much as among the good—and is sometimes stronger among the evil—and it is also found among beasts and birds, in whom no Charity can be formed. It is well known that this occurs among bears, tigers, and serpents, just as much as among sheep and goats, and among owls just as much as among doves. As specifically concerns the duties of parents toward children, these are inward...

Among those who are in Charity, that love is joined with love toward the neighbor and love for God; for by these people, children are loved according to their character, virtues, pursuits, and talents for serving the public. 432. **PRIVATE DUTIES OF CHARITY** are also numerous, such as paying wages to workers, paying interest, fulfilling agreements, safeguarding mortgages, and other similar things, some of which are duties based on forensic law, some on civil law, and some on moral law. These are also performed from a different mindset by those who are in Charity than by those who are not in Charity. By those who are in Charity, they are performed justly and faithfully; for it is a precept of Charity that one act justly and faithfully with everyone with whom they have any business or dealings (as discussed above in number 422 and following). But these same duties are performed in a completely different way by those who are not in Charity.

## *That the Social Gatherings of Charity are Luncheons, Dinners, and Social Circles.*

433. It is well known that Luncheons and Dinners are in use everywhere, and that they are established for various purposes: among many, they are for the sake of friendships, family ties, joy, profit, and rewards; they are also used as bribes to draw people into parties; and among the Great, they are for the sake of honor, and in the Courts of Kings for the sake of splendor. But **LUNCHEONS AND DINNERS of Charity** exist only among those who are in mutual love from a similar faith. In the Early Church <note>original: "Primitiva Ecclesia"; refers to the first few centuries of the Christian church after Christ</note> among Christians, Luncheons and Dinners were held for no other purpose, and they were called **FEASTS**, established so that they might be joyful together from the heart, and also be joined together. **DINNERS** <note>original: "Cænæ"; the evening meal</note> among them signified associations and conjunctions in the first state of the establishment of the Church, for the Evening, in which they occurred, signified that state; but **LUNCHEONS** <note>original: "Prandia"; the midday meal</note> signified the second state, when the Church was established, for the Morning and the Day signified that. At the tables, conversations were held on various subjects, both domestic and civil, but especially on such things as belonged to the Church. And because they were Feasts of Charity, Charity with its joys and gladness was present in the conversations on every subject. The spiritual sphere reigning in those Feasts was a sphere of love for the Lord and love toward the neighbor, which cheered everyone’s mind, softened the sound of every speech, and brought a festive feeling from the heart into all the senses; for from every person emanates a spiritual sphere, which is of the affection of their love and the thought from it, and it affects those present deep within—especially at Feasts. This sphere emanates both through the face and through the breathing. Since such associations of minds were signified by Luncheons and Dinners (or Feasts), they are therefore mentioned so often in the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Sacred Scripture or the Bible</note>, and in the spiritual sense nothing else is meant by them; and in the highest sense by the Paschal Supper <note>The Passover</note> among the children of Israel, and also by the banquets at the other Festivals, as well as by the eating of the Sacrifices near the Tabernacle. Conjunction itself was then represented by breaking bread and distributing it, and by drinking from the same cup and passing it to another.

434. As for **SOCIAL CIRCLES**, these existed in the Early Church among those who called themselves Brothers in Christ; therefore they were Social Circles of Charity, because they were a spiritual Brotherhood. They were also consolations for the adversities of the Church, rejoicings for its growth, and also recreations of the soul from studies and labors.

In these gatherings, Sycophants and Hypocrites stand at the stern and hold the tiller of the rudder in their hand.

## *That the First of Charity is to remove evils, and the Second is to do good things that are of use to the neighbor.*

435. In the <term>Doctrine of Charity</term> <note>The systematic teaching on how a person should love others according to divine law</note>, this holds the primary place: that the first part of <term>Charity</term> is not to do evil to the neighbor, and the second, to do good to him. This is a fundamental principle, serving as the door to the doctrine of Charity. It is well known that evil resides in the will of every human being from birth; and because all evil looks toward others both near and far, and also toward Society and the Country, it follows that inherited evil is evil against the neighbor in every degree. 

A person can see from reason itself that as long as the evil residing in the Will is not removed, the good that he does is impregnated with that evil; for evil is then inside the good, like a kernel in a shell or like marrow in a bone. Therefore, although the good done by such a person appears to be good, it is nevertheless not good on the inside. It is like a shiny shell within which the kernel has been eaten away by worms, or like a white almond that is rotten inside, from which rotten veins crawl out to the very surface. Willing evil and doing good are in themselves two opposites; for evil belongs to hatred against the neighbor, and good belongs to love toward the neighbor; or, evil is the neighbor's enemy, and good is his friend. 

These two cannot exist together in one mind—that is, evil in the <term>Internal man</term> <note>The inner self, or the spirit, which contains a person's true intentions</note> and good in the <term>External man</term> <note>The outer self, or the body and social persona, which acts in the world</note>. If they do coexist, the good in the External is like a wound treated only on the surface, while inside there is festering rot. Such a person is like a tree whose root is dead and yet still produces fruits that look tasty and useful on the outside, but are foul and useless inside. They are also like discarded dross which, polished and beautifully colored on the outside, is sold as precious stones. In a word, they are like the eggs of an owl, which people are led to believe are the eggs of a dove. 

A person should know that the good he does with the Body proceeds from his spirit, or from the <term>Internal man</term>. The <term>Internal man</term> is his spirit, which lives after death; therefore, when a person casts off the body (which constituted his External man), he is then entirely within his evils and finds his pleasure in them, and he turns away from good as something hostile to his life. That a person cannot do good that is good in itself before evil has been removed is taught by the Lord in many places: *They do not gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles; a rotten tree cannot produce good fruits*, Matthew 7:16, 17, 18. *Woe to you Scribes and Pharisees, you cleanse the outside of the cup and the plate, but the insides are full of plunder and intemperance. Blind Pharisee, cleanse first the inside of the cup and the plate, so that the outside may also become clean*, Matthew 23:25, 26. And

436. This can further be illustrated by these comparisons: no one can approach another person who keeps a leopard and a panther in his room—and because he feeds them, lives safely with them—unless he first removes those wild beasts. Who, when invited to the table of a King and Queen, would not first wash his face and hands before approaching? Who does not purify ores through fire, separating them from the dross, before receiving the pure gold and silver? That a person ought to purify himself from evils is comparatively like a servant coming before his master with his face and clothes stained with soot or dung, saying, "Master, wash me." Would not the master say to him, "Foolish servant, what are you saying? Look, there is water, soap, and a towel; do you not have hands and the power in them? Wash yourself!" And the Lord God will say: "The means of purification are from Me, and your will and power are also from Me; therefore, use these gifts and endowments of Mine as your own, and you shall be purified."

437. It is believed today that <term>Charity</term> <note>Defined here as the active spiritual love that flows from God into a person who has removed their own selfish evils</note> is simply doing good, and that if one does so, he does not do evil; consequently, that the first part of Charity is doing good, and the second is not doing evil. But it is entirely the reverse: the first part of Charity is to remove evil, and the second part is to do good. For it is a universal Law in the spiritual world, and from there also in the natural world, that so far as anyone does not will evil, he wills good; thus, as much as he turns himself away from hell—from which all evil ascends—so much does he turn himself toward Heaven, from which all good descends. Accordingly, as much as anyone rejects the devil, so much is he accepted by the Lord. No one can stand between the two with a "swivel neck," praying to one and the other at the same time; for these are they of whom the Lord says: *I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot; I wish you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am about to spit you out of my mouth*, Revelation 3:15, 16. Who can skirmish with his troop between two armies and favor both? Who can be in evil against his neighbor and simultaneously in good toward him? Does not the evil then hide itself in the good? Even if the evil that hides itself does not appear in outward acts, it nevertheless manifests itself in many ways when one reflects upon it rightly. The Lord says: *No servant can serve two masters; you cannot serve God and Mammon*, Luke 16:13.

438. But no one can purify himself from evils by his own power and his own strengths; yet it cannot be done without the power and strengths of the person *as if* they were his own. If these were not present, no one could fight against the flesh and its lusts, which is nevertheless commanded of everyone. Indeed, he would not even think of any struggle, but would let his mind loose into every kind of evil, and would be restrained from them in his actions only by the laws of justice established in the world and by their penalties. Thus, he would be like a tiger, a leopard, or a serpent within, which never reflect upon the cruel delights of their own loves. From this it is clear that because a human being is rational (unlike the wild beasts), he ought to resist evils by the power and strengths given to him by the Lord, which in every sense appear to him as his own. This appearance is given to every person by the Lord for the sake of <term>Regeneration</term>, <term>Imputation</term>, <term>Conjunction</term>, and <term>Salvation</term>. <note>These four terms represent the spiritual process: being born again, being credited with righteousness, being joined to God, and being saved from the power of hell.</note>

## That a person, in the exercises of Charity, should not place merit in Works, while he believes that all good is from the Lord.

439. To place <term>merit</term> <note>original: "meritum"; the idea that one has earned a reward from God through their own efforts</note> in works which are done for the sake of salvation is harmful; for in such a mindset, evils lie hidden of which the doer knows nothing. There is hidden a denial of the influence and operation of God within the person; a trust in one’s own power in matters of salvation; faith in oneself and not in God; self-justification; salvation from one's own strengths; the annihilation of Divine grace and mercy; the rejection of reformation and regeneration through Divine means. Specifically, it involves a detraction from the merit and justice of the Lord God the Savior, which the person instead claims for themselves. Furthermore, there is a constant looking toward a reward, which they regard as the first and final goal; the drowning and extinction of love for the Lord and love toward the neighbor; and a total ignorance and lack of perception regarding the joy of Heavenly love, which is without thought of merit, leaving only the sensation of self-love. For those who put reward in the first place and salvation in the second—thus pursuing the latter for the sake of the former—invert the proper order; they bury the interior desires of their mind in their own <term>proprium</term> <note>the "self" or ego; what is "one's own" as opposed to what is from God</note>, and defile them in the body with the evils of their own flesh. This is why good done for merit appears before the Angels like <term>rust</term> <note>original: "rubigo"; representing spiritual decay or the corrosive nature of the ego</note>, and good done without thought of merit appears like <term>purple</term> <note>original: "purpura"; in the Word, this color signifies the good of celestial love</note>. That good should not be done for the sake of reward, the Lord teaches in Luke: *If you do good to those who do good to you, what grace is that to you? Rather, love your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing in return; then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for He is kind to the ungrateful and the evil*, Chapter 6: 33 to 36. That a person cannot do good—which is good in itself—except from the Lord, is stated in John: *Abide in Me, and I in you; as the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you unless you abide in Me, for without Me you can do nothing*, Chapter 15: 4, 5. *And elsewhere: A man can receive nothing unless it has been given to him from Heaven*, Chapter 3: 27.

440. However, to think that they will come into Heaven, and that good should be done for that reason, is not to look at reward as the end goal or to place merit in works. For even those who love their neighbor as themselves and God above all things think this way, doing so out of faith in the Lord’s words: *That their reward shall be great in the Heavens*, Matthew 5: 11, 12; Chapter 6: 1; Chapter 10: 41, 42; Luke 6: 23, 25; Chapter 14: 12, 33, 34; John 4: 36. *That those who have done good works shall possess as an inheritance the Kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world*, Matthew 25: 34. *That to everyone it shall be rendered according to his works*, Matthew 16: 27; John 5: 29; Revelation 14: 13; Chapter 20: 12, 13; Jeremiah 25: 14; Chapter 32: 19; Hosea 4: 9; Zechariah 1: 6; and elsewhere. These people do not rely on a confidence in reward based on merit, but in a faith in the promise based on <term>grace</term>. For them, the delight of doing good to the neighbor is the reward itself; this is the delight the Angels have in Heaven, and it is a spiritual delight which is eternal and immensely exceeds every natural delight. Those who are in this delight do not wish to hear about merit, for they love to act, and they perceive a blessing in the doing; they are saddened if it is believed they act for the sake of a payout. They are like those who do good to friends for the sake of friendship, to a brother for the sake of brotherhood, to a wife and children for their own sake, or to one's country for its sake—acting thus out of friendship and love. Those who do good in this way also say and insist that they are not doing it for their own sake.

441. It is altogether different for those who look at reward in works as the very end goal. These are like people who enter into friendships for the sake of profit, and who also send gifts, perform services, and testify to their love as if from the heart; yet when they do not obtain what they hoped for, they turn away, renounce the friendship, and devote themselves to the person’s enemies and haters. They are also like Nurses, who suckle infants only for pay, and in the sight of the parents...

442. It must be clearly understood that Charity and Faith in the Lord are closely joined; therefore, as the Faith is, such is the Charity. *That the Lord, Charity, and Faith make one, just as life, will, and intellect do, and that if they are divided, each one perishes, like a union collapsed into dust*, may be seen above in number 362 and following. And *that Charity and Faith are together in good Works*, numbers 373 to 377. From this it follows, that as the Faith is, such is the Charity, and as the Faith and Charity are together, such are the works. Now, if the faith is that every good which a person does as if of themselves is from the Lord, then the person is the <term>instrumental cause</term> <note>the tool or means through which an action is performed</note> and the Lord the <term>principal cause</term> <note>the primary source or agent of the action</note>; these two causes appear before the person as one, even though the principal cause is the "all in all" of the instrumental cause. From this it follows that if a person believes that all good, which in itself is good, is done by the Lord, they do not place merit in works; and in that degree to which this faith is perfected in a person, the fantasy of **Merit** is taken away from them by the Lord. A person in this state performs exercises of Charity in abundance without fear of merit, and at last perceives the spiritual delight of Charity, and then begins to be averse to merit as something harmful to their life. Merit is easily wiped away by the Lord in those who imbue Charity by acting justly and faithfully in the work, business, and office in which they are, and with those with whom they have any dealings (concerning which see above, numbers 422, 423, 424). But merit is removed with difficulty from those who believe Charity is acquired through alms and giving help to the needy, for while they perform those things, first openly in their mind and then silently, they want a reward and attract merit.

443. Every person learns from parents and teachers to live morally, that is, to act as a civil person and exhibit the duties of honesty, which refer to various virtues (which are the essentials of honesty), and to produce them through its formalities, which are called decorum. ...[ado]lescence is natural, which then becomes more and more rational. Anyone who reflects well can see that a moral life is the same as the Life of Charity, which is to act well toward one's neighbor and to regulate life so it is not contaminated by evils; this follows from what was shown above in numbers 435 to 438. However, in the first period of life, a Moral Life is the Life of Charity in its extremes—that is, only its outer and forward-facing part, not its inner part. For there are four periods of life which a person passes through from infancy to old age: the FIRST is when one acts from others according to instructions; the SECOND is when one acts from oneself under the guidance of the intellect; the THIRD is when the Will acts into the Intellect, and the Intellect modifies that will; the FOURTH is when one acts from a confirmed purpose.

But these periods of life are the periods of the life of a person's spirit, not necessarily of their body. For the body can act morally and speak rationally, and yet the spirit can still will and think the opposite. That the natural man is like this is clearly evident from simulators, flatterers, liars, and hypocrites; it is obvious that these people enjoy a double mind, or that their mind is divided into two discordant parts. It is different for those who will well and think rationally, and from that basis act well and speak rationally; these are the ones meant by the <term>Simple in spirit</term><note>Latin: *simplices spiritu*. A reference to the "poor in spirit" or those with a single, honest purpose.</note> in the Word; they are called "simple" because they are not "double."

From this, it can be seen what is properly meant by the External and Internal man, and that no one can conclude the morality of the Internal man from the morality of the External man. The internal can be moving in the opposite direction and hide itself like a tortoise <note>original: *testudo*</note> hides its head in its shell, or like a snake hides its head in its coils. For such a so-called moral man is like a thief in a city who acts the part of a moral person, but in the forest acts as a robber. It is entirely different for those who are moral inwardly or as to their spirit, which happens through regeneration by the Lord; these are the ones understood as spiritual-moral people.

444. The reason why a moral life, when it is also spiritual, becomes a life of charity, is because the exercises of moral life and charity are the same. Charity is to will well toward the neighbor and from that to act well toward him; this is also the essence of moral life. The Spiritual Law is this one of the Lord: *All things whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you even so to them; this is the Law and the Prophets* (Matthew 7:12). This same law is the universal law of moral life. 

However, to list all the works of charity and compare them with the works of moral life would be a task of many pages; let the six commandments of the <term>Second Table</term><note>The portion of the Ten Commandments (the Decalogue) that deals with relationships with other people, traditionally starting with "Honor your father and mother."</note> of the Law of the Decalogue serve as illustration. It is clear to anyone that these are the precepts of moral life; and that they also contain everything belonging to love toward the neighbor may be seen above in numbers 329, 330, and 331. That Charity fulfills all of them is clear from these words of Paul: *Love one another, for he who loves another has fulfilled the Law; for this: you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not be a false witness, you shall not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is comprehended in this word: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. Charity does no evil to the neighbor; the fullness of the law is Charity* (Romans 13:8–10). 

He who thinks only from the External man cannot help but wonder why the seven commandments of the Second Table were promulgated by <term>Jehovah</term><note>The Hebrew name for God, used here to emphasize the divine origin of the law.</note> upon Mount Sinai with such a great miracle, when those same laws were already the precepts of civil justice in all kingdoms on earth—and thus also in Egypt, from which the children of Israel had recently come—for no kingdom can survive without them. But the reason they were promulgated by Jehovah, and moreover inscribed on stone tablets by His own finger, was so that they might be not only the precepts of civil society (and thus of a natural moral life), but also the precepts of celestial society (and thus of a spiritual moral life). Thus, to act against them would not only be to act against men, but also against God.

445. If Moral Life is viewed in its essence, it can be seen that it is a life according to both human and Divine laws simultaneously. Therefore, he who lives according to those two laws as One is a truly moral man, and his life is Charity. Anyone can...

## That a friendship of love, bound with a person regardless of their spiritual quality, is harmful after death.

446. By "friendship of love," I mean an interior friendship where not only the <term>External Man</term> is loved, but also the <term>Internal Man</term>, and this is done without examining what the person is like regarding their spirit—that is, the affections of their mind. We do not check whether they have love for their neighbor and for God (and are thus fit for the company of the angels of heaven), or whether they harbor hatred against their neighbor and God (and are thus fit for the company of devils). Many people form such friendships for various reasons and for various ends. This is distinct from an external friendship, which is focused only on the person's personality and exists for the sake of various pleasures of the body and senses, or for business dealings. This external friendship can be formed with anyone, even with a jester who tells jokes at a Duke’s table. This is called simply "friendship," but the former is called "friendship of love," because friendship is a natural conjunction, while love is a spiritual conjunction.

447. That a friendship of love is harmful after death can be seen from the state of heaven, the state of hell, and the state of a person's spirit respectively. Regarding the state of Heaven, it is divided into innumerable <term>Societies</term><note>Swedenborg describes heaven not as a single space, but as a vast network of communities organized by the specific "flavor" of love the inhabitants share.</note> according to all the varieties of the affections of the love of good; Hell, in turn, is divided according to all the varieties of the affections of the love of evil. After death, a person (who is then a Spirit) is immediately assigned to the society where their <term>ruling love</term> is, based on their life in the world. They go to a heavenly society if love for God and the neighbor formed the "head" of their loves, and to an infernal society if love of self and the world formed the "head" of their loves. Immediately after entering the spiritual world—which happens through death and the casting off of the material body into the grave—a person is prepared for a time for their specific society. This preparation happens by the casting off of loves that do not agree with their principal love. Because of this, friends are separated from friends, clients from patrons, parents from children, and brothers from brothers. Each is interiorly joined to those like themselves, with whom they will live a life that is conformed to their own and truly theirs for eternity. However, in the first period of preparation, they meet and converse in a friendly way just as they did in the world; but they are gradually pulled apart, which happens so slowly it is hardly noticed.

448. However, those who in the world bound themselves in a "friendship of love" cannot be separated according to this order and assigned to the Society corresponding to their life like others. Because they are interiorly bound as to their Spirit, they cannot be torn apart; they are like branches grafted onto other branches. Therefore, if one person is in Heaven as to their internal self, and the other is in Hell, they stick together much like a sheep tied to a wolf, or a goose to a fox, or a dove to a hawk. The one whose internals are in Hell breathes his hellish influences into the one whose internals are in Heaven. For among the things known in Heaven is this: that evils can be inspired into the good, but good cannot be inspired into the evil (this is because everyone is born into evil). Consequently, for the good who are so tightly bound to the evil, their internal minds are closed off, and both are dragged down into Hell. There, the good person suffers harshly, until finally, after a period of time, they are rescued and only then begin their preparation for Heaven. I have been allowed to see such bindings, especially between brothers and relatives, and also between masters and servants, and many people with flatterers, where they had opposite affections and different characters. I have seen some together like goats with leopards, kissing each other and swearing by their former friendship; and...

I heard that the good, when they were later rescued, were prepared for Heaven through means of reformation, though with more difficulty than others.

449. It happens quite differently with those who love the good in another—that is, those who love justice, judgment, sincerity, and benevolence out of <term>Charity</term><note>Charity here refers to a spiritual affection for doing what is right and helpful.</note>, and especially those who love faith and love toward the Lord. Because they love those things which are within a person, abstracted from those things which are outside of him, if they do not observe these same qualities in a person after death, they immediately withdraw from the friendship and are associated by the Lord with those who are in a similar state of good. It may be said that no one can explore the inner reaches of the mind of those with whom they are in company and commerce, but this is not necessary, provided a person guards themselves against a "friendship of love" with just anyone; an external friendship for the sake of various uses does no harm.

### *That there exists Spurious Charity, Hypocritical Charity, and Dead Charity.*

450. Genuine Charity, which is alive, does not exist unless it makes one with <term>Faith</term>, and unless both together look toward the Lord. For these three—the Lord, Charity, and Faith—are the three essentials of salvation. When they make one, Charity is Charity, and Faith is Faith, and the Lord is in them and they are in the Lord (see above, numbers 363 to 367, and numbers 368 to 372). However, where these three are not joined together, Charity is either spurious, or hypocritical, or dead. Since the time of its founding, there have been various <term>Heresies</term> in Christianity, and there are some today as well, in each of which these three essentials—God, Charity, and Faith—are acknowledged, for without those three there is no religion. As specifically concerns Charity, it can be attached to any heretical Faith; such as the faith of the <term>Socinians</term><note>A sect that denied the full divinity of Christ, viewing him as a divinely inspired man.</note>, the faith of the <term>Enthusiasts</term><note>Radical groups claiming direct, often emotional or mystical, personal revelation from God.</note>, the faith of the Jews, and even the faith of idolaters. All of these may believe their actions to be Charity because it appears similar in its external form; yet its quality changes according to the faith to which it is attached or joined; how this is so may be seen in the chapter on Faith.

451. Every Charity that is not joined to Faith in one God, in whom is the Divine Trinity, is **SPURIOUS**. Such is the Charity of the church today, whose Faith is in three Persons of the same Divinity in successive order—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Because they believe in three Persons, each of whom is a God subsisting by Himself, they believe in three Gods. Charity can be attached to this Faith (as has indeed been done by its defenders), but it can never be truly joined to it. Charity merely attached to such a faith is only natural and not spiritual, and is therefore spurious Charity. The same is true of the Charity of many other heresies, such as those who deny the Divine Trinity and therefore approach only God the Father, or only the Holy Spirit, or both of them apart from God the Savior. Charity cannot be joined to the faith of these people, and if it is joined or attached, it is Spurious. It is called Spurious because it is like offspring from an illegitimate bed, like the son of Hagar born to Abraham, who was cast out of the house (Genesis 21:9). Such Charity is like fruit not grown on a tree, but pinned to it with a needle; and it is like a chariot to which the horses are not harnessed, but only held by the reins in the hands of the driver—when they bolt, they pull the driver from his seat, leaving the chariot behind.

452. Moreover, **HYPOCRITICAL** Charity exists among those who, in churches and homes, humble...

They are like meat without blood; like ravens and parrots trained to speak words from some psalm; and like birds taught to sing the melody of a holy hymn: the sound of their speech is like the sound of a bird-catcher's whistle.

453. However, <term>Charity</term><note>Charity, in this theological sense, refers to the internal affection for doing good.</note> is DEAD among those whose <term>Faith</term> is dead, because Charity is of the same quality as Faith; that they make one was shown in the chapter on FAITH. That faith is dead in those who are without works is established from the Epistle of James, Chapter 3:17, 20 <note>Swedenborg likely refers here to the passage commonly found in James 2:17, 20, which states that faith without works is dead.</note>. Furthermore, Faith is dead in those who do not believe in God, but in men—both living and dead—and who worship idols as holy in themselves, just as the Pagans did of old. The offerings of those who hold this faith, which they spend on "miraculous images" (as they call them) for the sake of salvation, and which they count among the works of Charity, are no different than gold and silver placed in the urns and monuments of the dead; indeed, they are like morsels given to <term>Cerberus</term><note>The three-headed dog guarding the underworld in Greek mythology.</note> and payments to <term>Charon</term><note>The ferryman of the dead in Greek mythology.</note> to be transported into the <term>Elysian Fields</term><note>The final resting place of the virtuous in classical mythology.</note>. But the Charity of those who believe that God does not exist, but that Nature stands in place of God, is not spurious, nor hypocritical, nor dead, but it is NOTHING; for it is not joined to any faith. It cannot be called Charity, because its quality is defined by faith. The charity of such people, when viewed from Heaven, is like bread made from ashes, a cake made from fish scales, or like fruit made from wax.

## That the friendship of love among the evil is internal hatred between them.

454. It was shown above that every human being has an Internal and an External, and that his Internal is called the Internal man, and his External the External man. To this shall be added that the Internal man is in the spiritual world, and the External is in the natural world. The reason man was created this way is so that he can be associated with spirits and angels in their world, and thereby think analytically, and after death be transferred from his own world into the other. By the spiritual world, both Heaven and Hell are meant. Since the Internal man is in that world together with spirits and angels, and the External man is with other human beings, it is clear that a person can be associated with the spirits of Hell, and also be associated with the angels of Heaven. By this faculty and power, man is distinguished from beasts. A man is in himself such as he is regarding his Internal man, but not such as he is regarding the External, because the Internal man is his Spirit, which acts through the External. The material body, with which his Spirit is clothed in the natural world...

More on the Internal and External man may be seen above at number 401.

455. However, what a bad person is like regarding their Internal man, and what a good person is like regarding theirs, can be seen from this brief description of Hell and Heaven: for the Internal man in the wicked is joined to devils in Hell, and in the good it is joined to Angels in Heaven. Hell consists of its own Loves in the delights of all evils—that is, in the delights of hatred, revenge, and murder; in the delights of plundering and theft; in the delights of disparagement and blasphemy; in the delights of denying God and profaning the Word. These lie hidden in lusts upon which a person does not reflect; they burn with those delights like ignited firebrands; those are what are understood in the Word by infernal Fire. But the delights of Heaven are the delights of love toward the neighbor and love for God. Since the delights of Hell are opposite to the delights of Heaven, there is a great <term>Interstice<note>original: "Interstitium"; a gap or neutral middle ground.</note></term> between them, into which the delights of Heaven flow from above, and the delights of Hell from below. In the middle of this Interstice is man while he lives in the World, for the purpose of being in <term>Equilibrium<note>A state of balance that allows for spiritual choice.</note></term>, and thus in a **Free state** of turning himself toward Heaven or toward Hell. This Interstice is what is meant by the "great Chasm fixed" between those who are in Heaven and those who are in Hell (Luke 16:26). From these things it can be established what the friendship of love among the wicked is like: that regarding the External man, it is gestural and mimicking, and a simulation of morality, for the purpose of spreading its nets and exploring where the opportunity is given for enjoying the delights of their loves, from which their Internal man burns. It is only the fear of the law, and thus of reputation and life, which restrains them and inhibits their acts; therefore, their friendship is like a spider in sugar, a viper in bread, a crocodile chick in a honey cake, and a serpent in the grass. Such is the Friendship of the wicked with anyone. But among confirmed evildoers, such as among thieves, robbers, and pirates, it is a familiar friendship as long as they gape at plunder with a unanimous mind; for then they kiss each other as brothers, delight themselves with feasts, song, and dances, and conspire for the destruction of others. Yet indeed, each one looks deep inside himself at his companion as an enemy looks at an enemy; even the cunning plunderer sees this in his companion and fears it. From these things it is clear that among such people there is no friendship, but internal hatred.

455. <note>The number 455 is repeated in the original text.</note> Every person who has not openly given themselves over to evildoers and practiced plunder, but has led a civil, moral life for various useful ends, and yet has not restrained the lusts residing in the Internal man, may believe that their Friendship is not like this. But it is still so, in varying degrees, among all who have rejected faith and spurned the holy Church, regarding it as nothing for themselves but only for the common people. This has been given to be known for certain from many examples in the spiritual World. Among some of them, the delights of infernal love lay hidden like fires in scorched wood covered with bark; among some, like glowing coals under ashes; among some, like wax torches which flare up when fire is applied; and among others, differently. Such is every person who has rejected from their heart those things which belong to religion. The Internal man of these people is in Hell; and as long as they live in the World and remain ignorant of it because of the morality fashioned in external things, they acknowledge no others as neighbors except themselves and their own children. They look upon the rest either with contempt (and then they are like cats lying in wait for birds in nests) or with hatred (and then they are like wolves when they see dogs to devour). These things are brought forward so that it may be known what Charity is like in its opposite.

## On the Conjunction of love to God and love toward the neighbor.

456. It is well known that the Law promulgated from Mount Sinai was inscribed on two Tables, and that one of these concerns God and the other concerns Men; and that in the hand of Moses they were one Table, on the right side of which was the Writing concerning God, and on the left side that concerning men. Thus, when offered to the eyes of men, the writing of both parts could be seen at once; one part was in the sight of the other, just as it is read of Jehovah speaking with Moses and Moses with Jehovah face to face. This was done so that the Tables thus united might represent the <term>conjunction<note>A technical term in this theology for a spiritual "joining" or union between the Divine and the human.</note></term> of God with men, and the reciprocal conjunction of men with God. For this reason, the inscribed Law was called a **Covenant** and a **TESTIMONY**; <note>original: "Fædus & TESTIMONIUM"</note> "Covenant" signifies the joining together, and "Testimony" signifies a life lived according to the pact. From these two Tables thus united, one can see the conjunction of Love to God and Love toward the neighbor. The First Table involves all things that belong to Love to God, which primarily are: that one must acknowledge the one God, the Divinity of His Human, and the Holiness of the Word, and that He is to be worshiped through the holy things that proceed from Him. That this Table involves these things is evident from the commentary on the Commandments of the <term>Decalogue<note>The Ten Commandments.</note></term> in Chapter 5. The Second Table involves all those things that belong to Love toward the neighbor: its first five commandments involve those things that are of action and are called Works; the last two involve those things that are of the will, and thus those things which belong to Charity in its origin. In these last commandments, it is said *You shall not Covet*, and when a person does not covet those things that belong to the neighbor, he then wishes him well. *That the Ten Commandments of the Decalogue contain all things belonging to Love to God and Love toward the neighbor may be seen above in numbers 329, 330, and 331,* where it is also shown that the conjunction of both Tables exists in those who are in <term>Charity<note>In this context, "Charity" is not merely almsgiving, but the spiritual love of doing what is good and just.</note></term>.

457. It is otherwise with those who are in the Worship of God alone, and not simultaneously in Good works originating from Charity; these are like people who tear the covenant apart. It is different again with those who divide God into three and worship each one separately; and different still with those who do not approach God in His <term>Human<note>original: "Humano suo"; a reference to Swedenborg's doctrine that God must be approached through the person of Jesus Christ, the Divine Human.</note></term>. These are *those who do not enter through the door, but climb up some other way* (John 10:9). And it is different again with those who, by confirmation, deny the Divinity of the Lord. Among all these, there is no conjunction with God, and therefore no salvation; their Charity is nothing but spurious, and it does not join "face to face," but from the side or from behind. 

How this Conjunction occurs will also be briefly explained: God flows into every person with an acknowledgment of Himself into the knowledge people have of Him; and at the same time, He flows in with His Love toward men. The person who receives only the former (knowledge) and not the latter (love), receives that Inflow in the Understanding and not in the Will; he remains in knowledge without an interior acknowledgment of God, and his state is like a Garden in the time of winter. But the person who receives both the former and the latter receives the inflow in the Will and from there in the Understanding, and thus in the whole Mind; he has an interior acknowledgment of God which brings his knowledge of God to life. This person's state is like a Garden in the time of spring. The reason conjunction occurs through Charity is that God loves every single person, and because He cannot do good to them immediately, but does so mediately through other people, He inspires them with His love. He inspires this just as He inspires parents with love toward their children; and the person who receives that love is joined to God, and loves the neighbor from the love of God. In such a person, the Love of God is within the Love of the neighbor, making "to will" the same as "to be able." And because a person does no good unless it appears to him as if the being able, the willing, and the doing are from himself, this appearance is granted to him; and when he does it from freedom as if from himself, it is imputed to him and accepted as a reciprocal response, through which conjunction is made. This is like the relationship between the active and the passive, and the [completion] of this...

...cooperation, which occurs from what is active acting upon what is passive; and this relates in the same way as the Will relates to actions and Thought relates to speech, and as the Soul from the innermost part of the worker relates to both; it relates like <term>Effort<note>Latin: "Conatus." In this context, it refers to the internal force or tendency that produces motion.</note></term> in movement; and also like the prolific principle of a seed, which acts from the interior into the juices through which the tree grows even unto its fruits, and through the fruits produces new seeds; and it relates like Light in precious stones, which is reflected according to the textures of the parts, from which come various colors, as if they belonged to the stones, when nevertheless they belong to the light.

458. From these things it is clear where and of what quality the <term>Conjunction<note>A technical term for the spiritual union or "joining together" of the human and the Divine.</note></term> of love to God and love toward the neighbor is: that it is an inflow of God's Love toward men, and its reception by man and his cooperation therein is love toward the neighbor; in short, it is a conjunction according to these Words of the Lord: *On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in Me, and I in you* (John 14:20). And according to these Words: *He who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves Me, and I will love him, and will manifest Myself to him; and I will make my home with him* (John 14:21, 22, 23). All the Lord’s commandments refer to love toward the neighbor, which in summary are: not to do him evil, but to do him good; that they should love God, and God should love them, is according to those words of the Lord. Since those two Loves are so joined together, John says: *He who keeps the commandments of Jesus Christ remains in Him, and He in him. If anyone says, "I certainly love God," but hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see? This commandment we have from Him, that he who loves God, should also love his brother* (1 Epistle 3:24, and Chapter 4:20, 21).

459. To these things shall be added these **MEMORABLE RELATIONS**: <note>Latin: "Memorabilia." These are accounts of Swedenborg's experiences and visions in the spiritual world.</note> FIRST. I saw from a distance five <term>Gymnasia<note>Latin: "Gymnasia." These are spiritual schools of wisdom or academies where various intellectual and theological topics are discussed.</note></term>, which were surrounded by various kinds of light: the First by a flaming light, the Second by a yellow light, the Third by a bright white light, the Fourth by a light halfway between noon and evening, and the Fifth hardly appeared, for it stood as if in the shadow of evening. And I saw some people on the roads on horses, some in carriages, and some walking, and some running and hurrying; and these were going toward the First Gymnasium, which was surrounded by the flaming light. When I saw these things, a desire seized and drove me to go there and hear what was being debated there, wherefore I quickly prepared myself and joined those hurrying to the first Gymnasium, and I entered together with them; and behold, there was a great assembly, from which one part went to the right and another part to the left, to sit on benches along the walls. At the front I saw a low platform on which stood one who performed the office of President, who had a staff in his hand, a cap on his head, and a garment tinted with the flaming light of the Gymnasium. After they had gathered, he raised his voice and said, "Brothers, today discuss what <term>Charity<note>Latin: "Charitas." In this theology, Charity is defined as the internal affection for doing good to the neighbor.</note></term> is; each of you can know that Charity in its essence is spiritual, and in its exercises it is natural." And immediately one from the first bench on the left, where those who were considered wise were sitting, rose up and began to speak, saying: "My opinion is, **THAT MORALITY INSPIRED BY FAITH IS CHARITY**," and he confirmed it in this way: "Who does not know that Charity follows faith, just as a handmaid follows her mistress? <note>original: "pedissequa dominam"</note> and that a man who has faith performs the law, and thus Charity, so spontaneously that he does not know that it is Law and Charity that he lives, because if he knew it and did it in that way, and at the same time thought about salvation because of it, he would defile holy Faith with his own <insert>merit</insert>, and thus weaken its efficacy; is this not according to the dogma of our people?" And he looked toward those sitting at the sides, among whom were canons, and they nodded in agreement. "But what is spontaneous Charity, if not Morality, into which everyone is initiated from infancy, which therefore in itself is natural, but becomes spiritual when faith is inspired into it? Who can distinguish men by their moral life, whether faith is in them or not, for everyone lives morally? But God alone, who implants and seals faith..."

Having said these things, he took a fresh grape in his hand and said: "It is with Charity as it is with this grape; if you divide it, everything that is inside flows out," and he divided it, and it flowed out.

Afterward, one rose from the third bench on the right and spoke with a loud voice, saying: "My opinion is, **THAT CHARITY IS GIVING ALMS TO THE POOR AND BRINGING HELP TO THE NEEDY**; this is certainly Charity, because the Divine Word teaches this, whose command allows no contradiction. What is giving to the rich and those possessing wealth, if not vain glory, in which there is no Charity but only a vision of reward? In such giving, there is no genuine affection of love toward the neighbor, but a bastardized affection which is valued on Earth but not in the Heavens. Therefore, poverty and want are what must be assisted, because the idea of repayment does not enter into this. In the city where I lived, where I knew who were honest and who were wicked, I saw that all the honest people would stop at the sight of a poor person in the street and give alms; but all the wicked, seeing a poor person from the side, would pass by like blind men to the sight of him, and like deaf men to his voice. And who does not know that the honest have charity, and the wicked do not? He who gives to the poor and helps the needy is like a Shepherd who leads hungry and thirsty sheep into pasture and to drink; but he who only gives to the rich and those who have plenty is like one who worships <term>petty gods<note>Latin: "deastros." A derogatory term for minor or false deities.</note></term>, and forces food and wine upon those who are already gorged."

After him, one rose from the third bench on the left and speaking said: "My opinion is, **THAT CHARITY IS BUILDING HOSPITALS, INFIRMARIES, ORPHANAGES, AND GUESTHOUSES, AND SUSTAINING THEM WITH GIFTS**; I confirm this by the fact that such benefits and aids are public, and exceed private ones by many <term>parasangs<note>A "parasang" is an ancient Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles. Because Charity unites minds and makes one out of many, they called themselves 'Brothers'—but they were brothers in <note>original: "JESU CHRISTO Deo illorum"</note> JESUS CHRIST their God. But because they were then surrounded by the barbarous nations of the world, whom they feared, they made a community of their goods, from which they were cheered together and with one mind; in their social circles they spoke daily about the Lord God their Savior Jesus Christ, and at their lunches and dinners they spoke of Charity; hence their Brotherhood. But after their times, when schisms began to arise, and finally that loathsome <term>Arian Heresy<note>A 4th-century belief taught by Arius that denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ, suggesting he was a created being rather than co-eternal with God the Father.</note></term>, which among many people took away the idea of the Divinity of the Lord’s Human, Charity grew cold and the Brotherhood was scattered. It is true that all who worship the Lord in truth and do His commandments are brothers (*Matthew* 23:8), but they are brothers in spirit; yet because today no one is known for what they are in spirit, there is no need for people to call one another 'brothers.' A brotherhood of faith alone—and even less a brotherhood of faith in a god other than the Lord God the Savior—is not brotherhood, because charity, which creates it, is not in that faith. Therefore, I conclude that the old Christian Brotherhood was Charity; but this was, and is no longer; yet I prophesy that it is to come." When he said this, a flame-colored light appeared through the window from the east and tinted his cheeks, at the sight of which the assembly was struck with wonder.

Lastly, one rose from the fifth bench to the left and asked for permission to add some small contribution to these sayings, and after being granted leave, he said: "My opinion is, **THAT CHARITY IS TO FORGIVE EVERYONE THEIR OFFENSES**. I took this opinion from the common speech of those who approach the <term>Holy Supper<note>The sacrament of the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note></term>; for some then say to their friends, 'forgive me for what I have done wrong,' thinking thus that they have fulfilled all the duties of Charity. But I have thought to myself that this is merely a painted figure of Charity, and not the real form of its essence. For both those who do not forgive and those who do not follow charity with any effort say this; and these are not among those in the Prayer which the Lord himself taught: <note>original: "Pater remitte nobis delicta nostra, sicut nos remittimus delinquentibus contra nos"</note> *Father, forgive us our debts, as we forgive those who trespass against us.* For offenses are like ulcers, which, unless they are opened and healed, collect pus within them, which corrupts the surrounding parts, and like a serpent it creeps around and turns the blood everywhere into pus. It is the same with offenses against the neighbor; unless they are removed through repentance and through a life according to the Lord’s commandments, they remain and take root. And those who, without repentance, only pray to God to forgive them their sins, are like citizens of a city affected by a contagious disease who go to the Consul and say, 'Lord, heal us,' to whom the Consul would say, 'Why heal you? Go to a Physician, and find the remedies, and buy them from the pharmacist, and take them, and you shall be healed.' And the Lord says to those who pray for the forgiveness of sins without actual repentance: 'Open the Word, and read what I spoke through <note>original: "Esajam"</note> Isaiah: *Woe to the sinful nation, laden with iniquity; therefore when you spread forth your hands, I hide my eyes from you; even though you make many prayers, I do not hear. Wash yourselves, remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes, cease to do evil; learn to do good, and then your sins shall be removed and forgiven.*' (*Isaiah* 1:4, 15, 16, 17, 18)."

<meta>This page concludes a dramatic scene in the spiritual world where various definitions of charity have been debated. The narrator (Emanuel Swedenborg) provides the definitive synthesis, explaining that outward "good works" are only true charity if they are motivated by a spiritual love for justice and guided by wise judgment.</meta>

<page-num>294</page-num>

->UNIVERSAL THEOLOGY<-

<note>The text begins mid-word from the previous page: "Charity"</note>
**Charity** in its origin is spiritual, and in its derivation it is natural; and natural Charity, if it is spiritual within, appears before the Angels as transparent as a **Diamond**; but if it is not spiritual within, and therefore merely natural, it appears before the angels like a **Pearl** resembling the eye of a cooked fish. <note>In Swedenborg’s visionary language, a "cooked fish eye" represents something that looks like it has the form of life but is actually opaque and dead, lacking the light of spiritual truth.</note> It is not for me to say whether the famous examples of Charity which you have brought forth in order are inspired by spiritual Charity or not; but it is for me here to say what that "spiritual" element is which must be present, so that they may be natural forms of spiritual Charity. The spiritual essence itself of those acts is this: that they be done from a **love of justice with judgment**; that is, that a person, in the exercises of Charity, should see clearly whether they act from justice, and they see this through judgment.

For a person can do evil through "good deeds," and also do good through things that appear to be "evil deeds." For example, one does evil through good deeds if they supply a needy robber with money so that he may buy himself a sword—even if the robber does not say so when he begs; or if one rescues him from prison and shows him the way to the forest, saying to oneself, "It is not my fault that he commits robbery; I only gave help to a fellow human." To take another example: one who feeds a lazy person and protects him from being forced into labor, saying, "Come into a room of my house and lie in bed; why should you exhaust yourself?"—such a person encourages idleness. Then also, those who promote blood-relatives and friends of a dishonest character to positions of honor, in which they can plot many kinds of malice—who cannot see that such works of Charity do not come from any love of justice combined with judgment?

On the other hand, a person can do good through things that appear like evil deeds. For example: a Judge who acquits a criminal because he weeps and pours out words of piety, praying for a pardon because he is "his neighbor." Yet the Judge actually performs a work of Charity when he inflicts a penalty according to the law; for in this way he provides security so that the criminal does not do further evil, and ensures that Society—which is the "neighbor" in a higher degree—is not harmed, and that such a Judgment does not become a public scandal. Who does not also know that it serves the good of servants if they are corrected by their masters, and children by their parents, on account of their wrongdoings? It is the same with those in Hell, who all have a love for doing evil: they are kept shut in prison and are punished when they do evil—which the Lord permits for the sake of amendment. This is because the Lord is **Justice itself**, and from His own **Judgment** He does whatever He does.

From these things it can be seen why it was said above that spiritual Charity comes from a love of justice with judgment, but from a love coming from no other source than the Lord God the Savior. The reason is that every good of Charity is from the Lord; for He says: *He who abides in Me and I in him, this person bears much fruit, because without Me you can do nothing* <note>original: "Qui manet in Me & Ego in illo, hic fert fructum multum, quia sine Me non potestis facere quicquam"</note> (John 15:4); and that *to Him belongs all power in Heaven and on Earth* (Matthew 28:18); and every love of justice with judgment comes from no other source than the God of heaven, who is Justice itself, and from whom all Judgment comes to man (Jeremiah 23:5; 33:15). <note>The Latin text cites chapter 33:25, but the context refers to the "Righteous Branch" who executes judgment and justice mentioned in 33:15.</note>

From these points, let it be concluded that all those things said about Charity from the benches to the right and to the left—which were:
*   That Charity is Morality inspired by Faith;
*   That it is Piety inspired by pity;
*   That it is doing good to the virtuous and the wicked alike;
*   That it is serving blood-relatives and friends in every way;
*   That it is giving to the poor and helping the needy;
*   That it is building <term>hospitals<note>original: "Nosocomia"; referring generally to institutions for the sick, poor, or infirm.</term></note> and supporting them with gifts;
*   That it is enriching Churches and doing good to their Ministers;
*   That it is the old Christian Brotherhood;
*   That it is forgiving everyone their sins;

—all these are excellent examples of Charity when they are done from a **love of justice with judgment**. Otherwise, they are not Charity; they are merely like streams separated from their fountain, or like branches torn from their tree. For genuine Charity is to believe in the Lord, and to act justly and rightly in every work and duty. Whoever, therefore, loves Justice from the Lord and acts upon it with judgment, that person is Charity in the Lord's image and likeness.

After these things were proclaimed, a silence fell, such as occurs among those who see and acknowledge something to be true with their **Internal man**, but not yet in their **External man**; I noticed this from their faces. But suddenly I was then taken away from their sight, for from the spirit I re-entered into my— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "manuscript" or "body."</note>

He concludes that outward acts only become genuine charity when they are performed by looking to the Lord and acting rightly in one's daily duties.</summary>

...my material body; for the natural man, because he is clothed with a material body, does not appear to any spiritual man (that is, to a spirit or angel), nor the reverse.

460. **THE SECOND MEMORABLE RELATION** <note>In Swedenborg’s writings, a "Memorable Relation" (Memorabile) is a narrative account of things he claims to have seen and heard in the spiritual world, intended to illustrate theological points.</note>. Once, when I looked around in the spiritual world, I heard something like the gnashing of teeth, and also a rhythmic knocking, and mixed in with them a kind of rasping sound. I asked what they were, and the Angels who were with me said: "They are Colleges, which we call 'Lodgings,' where people debate with one another. Their debates are heard this way from a distance, but when you are close, you hear only the arguments." I approached and saw small huts woven from reeds and stuck together with mud. I wanted to look in through a window, but there was none; for it was not permitted to enter through the door, because the Light from Heaven would flow in and cause confusion.

But suddenly a window was made on the right side, and I heard them complaining that they were in darkness. Soon, however, a window was made on the left side, and the window on the right was closed; then the darkness was gradually scattered, and they seemed to themselves to be in their own light. After this, I was permitted to enter through the door and listen. There was a table in the middle and benches all around, yet they all appeared to me to be standing on the benches and arguing sharply with one another about **FAITH** and **CHARITY**. On one side, they argued that Faith was the Essential of the Church; on the other, that Charity was.

Those who made Faith the Essential said: "Do we not act with God through Faith, and with man through Charity? Is Faith not therefore heavenly, and Charity earthly? Are we not saved through heavenly things and not through earthly things? Furthermore, cannot God give Faith from Heaven because it is heavenly, and must not man give himself Charity because it is earthly? What a man gives himself is not of the Church, and therefore does not save. Can anyone be justified before God by works, which are called the works of Charity? Believe us, we are justified and even sanctified by Faith alone, provided that Faith is not defiled by the claim of merit, which comes from the works of Charity," and more besides.

But those who made Charity the Essential of the Church sharply refuted these points, saying: "Charity saves, and not Faith. Does God not hold everyone dear and will good to everyone? How can God do this except through men? Does God only grant us to speak with men about things of Faith, and not grant us to do for men things of Charity? Do you not see that you have spoken absurdly of Charity as being earthly? Charity is Heavenly; and because you do not perform the good of Charity, your Faith is earthly. How do you receive your Faith, except as if you were a log or a stone? You say it is through the hearing of the Word; but how can the Word, once heard, operate, and how can it operate upon a log or a stone? Perhaps you are made alive while being completely unaware of it; but what is that 'making alive,' except that you can say that Faith alone justifies and saves? But what Faith is, and what saving Faith is, you do not know."

But then a man stood up, who was called a **Syncretist** <term>Syncretist: One who attempts to reconcile or combine different, often opposing, beliefs or schools of thought.</term> by the Angel speaking with me. He took a cap and placed it on the table, but suddenly put it back on his head because he was bald. He said: "Listen! You are all in error. It is true that Faith is spiritual and Charity is moral, but they are nonetheless joined together; and they are joined through the Word, and then through the Holy Spirit, and through the Effect, which can indeed be called Obedience, but in which man has no part; for when Faith is brought in, man knows no more than a statue. I have thought about these things with myself for a long time, and I have finally found that man can receive Faith from God which is spiritual, but he cannot be moved by God to a Charity which is spiritual any more than a log can."

At these words, those who were for Faith alone applauded, but those for Charity hissed. The latter said in indignation: "Listen, comrade! You do not know what a spiritual moral life is, or what a merely natural moral life is. A spiritual moral life exists among those who do good from God, and yet as if from themselves; while a merely natural moral life exists among those who do good from Hell, and yet likewise as if from themselves."

...to those who made Charity the only Essential of the Church, and the rasping noise mixed in was from the Syncretist <note>A syncretist attempts to reconcile different or opposing beliefs, often at the expense of theological clarity.</note>; the reason their sounds were heard as such from afar was because they all debated while in the World and did not shun any evil, and therefore did not do any good of spiritual lineage; and also they were completely ignorant that everything of Faith is truth, and everything of Charity is good, and that Truth without good is not Truth in spirit, and that good without truth is not Good in spirit, and that thus the one makes the other.

461. **THE THIRD MEMORABLE RELATION:** Once in spirit I was carried forward into the southern Quarter in the spiritual World, and into a certain Paradise there, and I saw that this one excelled the others I had surveyed until now; the reason was that a Garden signifies Intelligence, and all those who excel others in intelligence are transferred to the South. The Garden of Eden, in which Adam was with his Wife, signifies nothing else; wherefore, their being expelled from it involves being expelled from intelligence, and thus also from integrity of life. While I was walking in this southern Paradise, I noticed some people sitting under a certain laurel eating figs; I went over to them and asked them for figs, and they gave me some; and behold, the Figs in my hand became Grapes. While I wondered at this, an angelic Spirit who stood near me said, "The Figs in your hand have become Grapes, because Figs from correspondence <note>A core concept in Swedenborg's work, where natural objects represent specific spiritual realities.</note> signify the goods of Charity and thus of Faith in the natural or external man, but Grapes signify the goods of Charity and thus of Faith in the spiritual or internal man; and because you love spiritual things, it happened so for you; for in our World all things happen and exist, and also change, according to correspondences."

Immediately then there came upon me a greed for knowing how a man can do good from God, and yet entirely as if from himself; therefore I asked those eating figs how they understood it. They said they could not understand it otherwise than that God works it inside a man, and through a man when he does not know it, since if a man were conscious of it and did it thus, he would only do apparent good, which is evil inside; for everything that proceeds from man proceeds from his own <term>proprium</term> <note>A Latin term meaning "that which is one's own," used here to describe the inherent self-centered nature of humanity.</note>, and this is evil from birth. How then can good from God and evil from man be joined, and thus proceed jointly into action? Moreover, the human selfhood in matters of salvation continually breathes merit <note>original: "meritum"; the idea that one's own actions deserve a spiritual reward from God.</note>, and as much as it does this, it takes away from the Lord His own merit, which is the height of injustice and impiety. In a word, if the good that God works in man were to flow into man’s willing and thus into his doing, that good would be completely defiled and also profaned, which God never permits. A man can indeed think that the good he does is from God, and call it the good of God through himself, but still, how it happens, we do not understand.

But then I opened my mind and said, "You do not understand because you think from appearance, and thought from appearance confirmed is a fallacy. The appearance and the resulting fallacy for you is because you believe that all things which a man wills and thinks, and thus does and speaks, are in himself, and consequently from himself, when yet nothing of them is in him except the state of receiving what flows in. Man is not life in himself, but is an organ receiving life; the Lord is Life in Himself, as He also says in John:
> *Just as the Father has Life in Himself, so also He has given to the Son to have Life in Himself, Chapter 5:26.*
besides elsewhere, as in *John 11:25* and *Chapter 14:6, 9.* There are two things that make Life: Love and Wisdom, or what is the same, the Good of love and the Truth of wisdom; these flow in from God and are received by man as if they were his own, and because they are felt that way, they also proceed from man as if his own. That they are felt thus by man is granted by the Lord, so that what flows in may affect him, and thus be received and remain. But because all evil also flows in, not from God but from Hell, and this is received with delight because man is born such an Organ, therefore no more good is received from God than the amount of evil that is removed by the man as if by himself, which is done through Repentance, and at the same time through Faith in the Lord." That Love and Wisdom, Charity and Faith, or more generally speak—
